anatomy.title: Anatomy of a component
anatomy.lead: A Xaendar component is a standard custom element: a class extending CustomElement, decorated with @WebComponent, plus an HTML template and an optional stylesheet. The compiler turns the template into a render function at build time; at run time the browser creates, connects and removes the element like any other tag.

threeFiles.title: Three files
threeFiles.p1: The suffix of the class file is not a convention but a requirement: the Vite plugin only compiles the classes declared in files ending with .xd.component.ts. The template and the stylesheet can have any name, since the decorator points to them.
threeFiles.p2: Everything a component needs is in the example above:
threeFiles.li1: state in signals (value, hovered): writing one updates exactly the nodes that read it;
threeFiles.li3: event handlers in methods, called by the template with (click)="rate(star)";
threeFiles.li4: constants in plain members (stars): the template reads them, but nothing is notified when they change. See Shared state for the rule.
threeFiles.p3: The template reads the public members of the class by name, without this. It is type-checked against the class at build time: a misspelled member or a wrong argument fails the build.

theDecorator.title: The decorator
theDecorator.td2: The tag name of the component. See Selectors and registration.
theDecorator.td4: The template, relative to the class file.
theDecorator.td6: A .css, .scss, .sass or .less file relative to the class file. See Styling.
theDecorator.p1: The decorator does two things at run time: it stores the selector in the metadata of the class, where @Query(Class) finds it, and it calls customElements.define(selector, Class). The rest happens at build time, where the plugin reads the three options straight from the source code.

theBaseClassAnd.title: The base class and the shadow root
theBaseClassAnd.p1: CustomElement extends HTMLElement. Its constructor attaches an open shadow root, where the template is rendered: the page styles do not reach inside it, and the component styles do not leak out. The template is rendered each time the element is connected to the document, and the shadow root is emptied each time it is removed. The Lifecycle page covers the hooks in between.
theBaseClassAnd.example1: What the base class sets up
theBaseClassAnd.p2: The class is a real HTMLElement: document.createElement('ex-rating') returns an instance of RatingComponent, and every DOM API (attributes, events, classList, ...) works on it as on a native element.

generics.title: Generic components
generics.p1: A component class can have type parameters. The types of its inputs and of its outputs are then checked against the types TypeScript infers from the values bound to the inputs, as it does for a function call: items="{rows()}" gives Item the type of the rows, so $event of selected carries it too.
generics.p2: The type arguments can also be written explicitly, between parentheses right after the tag name, as a directive writes them between angle brackets: <ex-picker(Row, number)>. They give the first type parameters, in order. As TypeScript does for a function call, nothing is inferred then: the type parameters left out take their default type (Key = string), and leaving out one without a default type is an error. Without type arguments, a type parameter nothing is inferred for takes its default type, or any when it has none. A constraint is checked on the given or inferred type, reported on the type arguments or on the tag name. More type arguments than type parameters, or type arguments on a component that is not generic or on a native element, are an error. Type parameters are only for the type-check: they have no effect at runtime.

callout1.heading: Options must be string literals
callout1.p1: The plugin reads selector, templateUrl and styleUrl from the source code, so they must be string literals, and the class must be declared in a file ending with .xd.component.ts. A constant, a template literal or a computed value fails the build, and so does a component declared in another file.

callout2.heading: A missing template fails the build
callout2.p1: A templateUrl pointing to a file that does not exist fails the build. In the dev server the error is printed in the terminal and the component is served without its template, so connecting it throws, until the file is created: the component is then compiled again.

callout3.heading: Created is not rendered
callout3.body: An element created with document.createElement has a shadow root, but an empty one: the template is rendered on connection, and removed on disconnection. The inspector above shows the three states.

callout4.heading: Private and protected members are out of reach
callout4.p1: The template is type-checked as code outside the class, so it can only read public members. A private or protected member fails the build.

callout5.heading: Member names already taken by HTMLElement
callout5.body: The class inherits every member of HTMLElement, so a signal named title, an input named lang or an event named remove clashes with it, and TypeScript rejects the class. The build type-checks templates, not classes, so the error only shows in the editor or with tsc. See the edge cases of Outputs for the fixes.

callout6.heading: Closed shadow roots
callout6.p1: The shadow root is always open, and it cannot be replaced: the base class has already attached it.

contentProjection.title: Content projection with slots
contentProjection.lead: The elements written between the tags of a component are not rendered inside it: they stay where they are, as children of the element, and the component shows them through the <slot> elements of its template. Xaendar adds nothing to the standard slots of the shadow DOM, so everything you know about them applies.

defaultSlotNamedSlots.title: Default slot, named slots and fallback
defaultSlotNamedSlots.p1: A <slot /> without a name receives every child without a slot attribute. A <slot name="header" /> receives the children with slot="header". The content of a slot is its fallback, shown while nothing is assigned to it.
defaultSlotNamedSlots.p2: The second card fills only the default slot, so its header shows Untitled. The footer of the first card is projected inside an @if: projected content is part of the template of the parent, with its conditions, its loops and its bindings. The button in the footer calls a method of the parent and shows a signal of the parent; the card only decides where it appears.

choosingTheSlotAt.title: Choosing the slot at run time
choosingTheSlotAt.p1: slot is an attribute like any other, so it can be bound to an expression: the browser moves the element to the new slot when the value changes. An element whose slot matches no slot of the component is not shown at all.
choosingTheSlotAt.p2: On nowhere the note disappears, but it is still a child of the split view: its bindings keep running, and it shows up again as soon as its slot matches.

forwardingSlots.title: Forwarding slots
forwardingSlots.p1: A component can pass its projected content on to a child component: it puts a <slot> among the children of the child, with a slot attribute choosing where it goes.
forwardingSlots.example1: A panel forwarding its slots to a card
forwardingSlots.p2: The second panel receives no title, and shows Panel fallback, not the Untitled of the card: the card receives the slot of the panel, so for the card its header is never empty.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: The component is rendered before the parent creates its children, so in afterRender its slots are still empty. The children arrive right after, and every change is announced by slotchange, which a template can bind on the <slot> element. To read the projected elements reactively, use a content query.

callout1.heading: Whitespace does not hide the fallback
callout1.body: In plain HTML the spaces and line breaks between the tags of a component are text nodes, assigned to the default slot, so the fallback disappears. A Xaendar template creates no text node for whitespace, and the anchors of @if and @for are comments, which are never assigned: as long as nothing visible is projected, the fallback shows.

callout2.heading: Projected content belongs to the parent
callout2.body: The component cannot read the projected elements through its template, nor style them beyond ::slotted(): they are elements of the template of the parent, styled by its stylesheet. See Styling.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: The default slot: the children without a slot attribute.
summary.td2: A named slot: the children with slot="x".
summary.td3: Shows its content while nothing is assigned to it.
summary.td4: Moves a child to another slot when the value changes.
summary.td5: Fires on a slot when the elements assigned to it change.

contentQueries.title: Content queries
contentQueries.lead: A content query finds elements among the content projected into the component, instead of its own template. It is how a component works with children it does not render: a tab group with its panels, a list with its items, a form with its fields. Like view queries, the result is a signal that follows the changes of the content.

queryingTheProjectedContent.title: Querying the projected content
queryingTheProjectedContent.p1: @Query.content and @Query.content.all take the same targets as view queries, a CSS selector, the class of a component or the class of a custom directive, and look into the elements assigned to the slots of the component, together with their descendants.
queryingTheProjectedContent.example1: A tab group built from its panels
queryingTheProjectedContent.p2: The group renders one tab for each panel it finds, with the label the panel received from the parent, and tells each panel whether it is active through a signal of the panel: the query is typed by the class, so the group can reach the public members of the instances. Add a panel: the parent renders it inside the group, the query finds it, and a new tab appears.
queryingTheProjectedContent.p3: @Query.content.required drops null from the type, and reading it throws when no projected element matches. The projected content arrives after afterRender (see the edge cases below), so there it still throws: read it in event handlers, and keep @Query.content to follow the content as it arrives.

whichSlotsWhichElements.title: Which slots, which elements
whichSlotsWhichElements.p1: By default a content query looks into every slot. slots restricts it to one slot, or to a list, where the empty string is the default slot; lightDom: true looks instead at all the children of the element, assigned to a slot or not. The two options cannot be combined.
whichSlotsWhichElements.example1: Five queries on the same content
whichSlotsWhichElements.li1: the results follow the slots in the order of the template, then the order of assignment: aside comes first in the inspector, so B comes before A, even though A comes first in the parent;
whichSlotsWhichElements.li2: descendants count: C is inside a div assigned to the default slot;
whichSlotsWhichElements.li3: D is assigned to no slot: only lightDom finds it, in document order;
whichSlotsWhichElements.li4: E is the fallback of a slot: it belongs to the inspector, and no content query finds it.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: The wrapper projects its own slot into the counter. The query of the counter does not see that slot but what it carries: the items written in the outermost template, then the item of the wrapper. Nested slots are flattened.

callout1.heading: Empty until after afterRender
callout1.body: The projected content is created by the parent after the component has rendered, so in afterRender a content query is still empty. Read it reactively, in a computed signal or in an effect, as the tab group does. See the edge cases of Content projection.

callout2.heading: Attribute changes are not observed
callout2.body: A content query is updated when elements are added or removed, when their slot attribute changes and when the slots of the component change. A change to any other attribute, such as a class, does not update it, as for view queries.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: The first projected element matching target, or null.
summary.td2: All the projected elements matching target.
summary.td3: Only the given slots; '' is the default slot.
summary.td4: All the children of the element, assigned to a slot or not.
summary.td5: Like @Query.content, without null: reading it throws when no element matches.

domApis.title: Using DOM APIs
domApis.lead: Templates cover most of the DOM work, but not all of it: drawing on a canvas, moving the focus, measuring elements, driving a library that knows nothing about signals. For those, a component combines three tools: a query to reach the element, a lifecycle hook to know when it exists, and an effect to keep it in sync with the state.

drawingFromTheState.title: Drawing from the state
drawingFromTheState.p1: An effect created in afterRender runs once the template exists, and again whenever a signal it reads changes. It is disposed when the component is disconnected, and created again at the next connection, with the new elements.
drawingFromTheState.example1: A canvas redrawn by an effect
drawingFromTheState.p2: The effect reads values and color, so each button redraws the chart exactly once. Nothing else in the component knows about the canvas.

reactingToElementsThat.title: Reacting to elements that come and go
reactingToElementsThat.p1: A query is a signal, so an effect reading it runs again when the element appears or disappears. Created in onInit, the effect follows the element for the whole life of the component.
reactingToElementsThat.example1: Focus the field as soon as it appears
reactingToElementsThat.p2: Edit only changes a signal: the @if renders the field, the query finds it, and the effect focuses it. The same pattern works for scrolling an element into view or starting an animation.

observers.title: Observers
observers.p1: ResizeObserver, IntersectionObserver and MutationObserver connect to elements of the template in afterRender and disconnect in onDestroy. Their callbacks write signals, and the template does the rest.
observers.example1: A box that knows its width
observers.p2: Listeners on window or document follow the same rule: add them in onInit and remove them in onDestroy, through a stable reference. Listeners on elements of the template need no cleanup: they go away with the elements.

customElementsFromOther.title: Custom elements from other libraries
customElementsFromOther.p1: A template can use an element of another library once its tag is declared in customElements (see Selectors and registration), but its bindings write attributes, which carry only strings. To pass any other value to a property, create the element in code: in afterRender, inside an element of the template, with an effect copying the state into its properties.
customElementsFromOther.example1: A custom element written without Xaendar
customElementsFromOther.p2: The gauge is a plain HTMLElement with a value property, as a component of any other library would be. The effect sets the property, not an attribute, so any type of value can be passed. The gauge is created with new VanillaGauge(): with document.createElement the class would be used only as a type, TypeScript would drop the import, and the element would never be defined.

callout2.heading: Imperative changes to bound attributes do not last
callout2.body: An attribute bound in the template is written again whenever its value changes: a class added with classList to an element whose class is bound is gone at the next update. Change the state the binding reads instead, or touch only what the template does not bind.

callout4.heading: Do not move the elements of the library
callout4.body: The library creates, moves and removes the elements of the templates and the components. Moving, removing or reattaching them with the DOM APIs is not supported: change only the elements you created yourself, as the gauge above.

inheritance.title: Inheritance
inheritance.lead: Components are classes, so they can share logic through a base class: signals, computed signals, methods, inputs and events are inherited as usual, and templates can read and bind them. The template is not inherited: it belongs to each decorated class.

aBaseClassFor.title: A base class for shared logic
aBaseClassFor.p1: The base class extends CustomElement and has no decorator: it is not a component, and it is never registered. Each component extends it, with its own @WebComponent and its own template.
aBaseClassFor.p2: count, atZero and the three methods live in CounterBase; the two templates read them as if they were declared in the components. Signals declared in a base class are recognized in attribute bindings too: the compiler follows the extends chain, also into other files.
aBaseClassFor.p3: Inputs and events are inherited too. CounterBase declares step with @Property, and the compiler checks step="{ 5 }" against its type, as if the input were declared in the component.

extendingAComponent.title: Extending a component
extendingAComponent.p1: A component can extend another one. The subclass needs its own decorator, which gives it a selector and a render function; its templateUrl can point to the template of the parent. The options of the decorator are not inherited: the hostDirectives of the parent are listed again in the one of the subclass, if it needs them.

callout3.heading: A subclass without a decorator has no template
callout3.p1: The render function belongs to the decorated class, and it is not looked up along the prototype chain. A subclass registered by hand, without @WebComponent, throws when it is connected.

callout4.heading: The base class needs no file suffix
callout4.body: Only the classes decorated with @WebComponent must be in .xd.component.ts files. A base class without decorator can live in any file, as counter-base.ts does.

inputs.title: Inputs with @Property
inputs.lead: An input is how a parent passes data to a child. You declare it with @Property on an accessor of the child, and it becomes an InputSignal: a signal that the parent writes through its template and the child can only read. Everything that reads it, in the template or in a computed signal, updates when the parent binds a new value.

declaringAnInput.title: Declaring an input
declaringAnInput.p1: The decorator goes on an accessor field typed InputSignal<T>, which the decorator replaces with the signal; the ! tells TypeScript that the field is initialized for you. The first argument is the default value, used until the parent binds something. The name used in templates is the name of the accessor, unless alias gives another one: an alias is the way to use dashes, as HTML attributes usually do.
declaringAnInput.p2: The first meter binds all three inputs; the second binds only value, so max stays 100 and show-value stays true. Inside the meter, percent is a computed signal reading two inputs: inputs are signals like any other, so everything built on them is reactive.
declaringAnInput.p3: The type of the input can be any type, imported ones included: the templates binding it are checked against it. TypeScript infers the type of the decorator from the default value, so a default such as 'ts', [] or null gives a type that does not match the accessor. Pass the type of the signal to the decorator too, instead of widening the accessor and casting the value where you read it.

staticValuesAndExpressions.title: Static values and expressions
staticValuesAndExpressions.p1: A binding on a component tag sets the input, not an attribute. Its value is either the text written in the template, always a string, or the result of an expression in braces, of any type. The template compiler checks both against the type of the input.
staticValuesAndExpressions.example1: A static value and an expression
staticValuesAndExpressions.p2: The input of ex-value-type is InputSignal<unknown>, so both bindings compile, and the child receives a string in the first case and a number in the second. On an input typed number the static value does not compile:

normalizingAndComparingTransform.title: Normalizing and comparing: transform and equals
normalizingAndComparingTransform.p1: transform runs on every value the parent binds, before it is stored. equals compares the result with the current value: when it returns true the input keeps its value and notifies nobody. By default the comparison is Object.is, so a new array with the same content counts as a change.
normalizingAndComparingTransform.example1: Tags trimmed, lowercased and compared by content
normalizingAndComparingTransform.p2: Send the same tags binds a new array, but once normalized it has the same tags as the current one: the count of runs does not move. Send other tags moves it by one. The first run of the effect happens in onInit, and reads the tags already bound by the parent.

requiredInputs.title: Required inputs
requiredInputs.p1: @Property.required() declares an input without a default. Every template using the component must bind it, and the check happens at build time: a template that leaves it out fails to compile, and so does a template that binds it only in some branches of a conditional binding.

whenTheValuesArrive.title: When the values arrive
whenTheValuesArrive.p1: The parent binds the inputs of a child, and the listeners of its events, before inserting it in the page. So in onInit, in the first render and in afterRender, every input already has its bound value, required ones included. When a bound value changes later, everything that reads the input reactively updates.
whenTheValuesArrive.example1: What the card sees, step by step
whenTheValuesArrive.p2: Add the card and read the log: onInit, the effect and afterRender all see the bound name. Rename re-runs only the effect, and the text of the card. Hence the rule:
whenTheValuesArrive.li1: read inputs reactively: in the template, in computed signals and in effects, never once in a hook;

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: When the condition of a conditional binding stops holding, the input goes back to its default, 50, not to the last bound value. Binding it again sets the current value of the parent.

callout1.heading: Attributes written from outside are ignored
callout1.body: An input is not linked to the attribute of the same name: there is no attributeChangedCallback. The button of the second example writes value="42" on the first component, and nothing changes. Code outside Xaendar cannot set an input through the DOM: give the component a method, or wrap it in a Xaendar parent.

callout2.heading: Inputs are read-only inside the component
callout2.p1: InputSignal has no public set: only the bindings of the parent write it. For a value that the component changes too, copy the input into a local signal in an effect, and write the local one.

callout3.heading: transform does not change the type checked in templates
callout3.p1: Templates are checked against the type of the InputSignal, not against the parameter of transform: a transform from string to number does not let you write a static number. Use transforms that keep the type, and bind expressions.

callout5.heading: A component defined after its parent rendered
callout5.body: A component loaded later, for example with a dynamic import, receives its bindings as string attributes until it is defined, and its default values after. See Selectors and registration.

lifecycle.title: Lifecycle
lifecycle.lead: A component is rendered when its element is connected to the document and torn down when it is disconnected. Three optional methods let you run code at those moments: onInit, afterRender and onDestroy. They run at every connection and disconnection, not once per element.

theHooks.title: The hooks
theHooks.td1: Once, when the element is created.
theHooks.td2: Rarely needed: fields are initialized here anyway.
theHooks.td3: At every connection, before the render.
theHooks.td5: At every connection, after the render.
theHooks.td6: Work on the elements of the template: focus, measures, canvas, third-party libraries.
theHooks.td7: At every disconnection, before the template is removed.
theHooks.td8: Undoing what onInit did outside the component.
theHooks.p1: The effects created with this.effect() need no cleanup: they are disposed when the element is disconnected, right after onDestroy. The full sequence:

parentsAndChildren.title: Parents and children
parentsAndChildren.p1: A child component is connected while its parent renders its template, once the parent has bound its inputs and its listeners. So the child runs its whole sequence, from onInit to afterRender, in the middle of the sequence of the parent, already seeing the bound values.
parentsAndChildren.example1: The hooks of a parent and its child
parentsAndChildren.p2: Add the parent and read the log from the top: the parent starts, the child runs all its hooks and its effect with the bound label, then the parent finishes. Changing the label re-runs only the effect. Removing the parent calls onDestroy on the parent first, then on the child, and disposes the effect of the child.

callout2.heading: connectedCallback and disconnectedCallback are taken
callout2.p1: The base class uses the callbacks of custom elements to render the template, and keeps them private. Defining them in a component does not compile, and at run time would replace the ones of the base class: the template would never be rendered. Use the hooks.

callout4.heading: No attributeChangedCallback
callout4.body: Inputs are not attributes, so the base class declares no observedAttributes: read inputs reactively instead. See Inputs.

summary.td1: Runs at every connection, before the render.
summary.td2: Runs at every connection, after the render and the start of the view queries.
summary.td3: Runs at every disconnection, before the effects are disposed and the template is removed.
summary.td4: An effect disposed at the next disconnection. Returns a function that disposes it earlier.

outputs.title: Outputs with @Event
outputs.lead: An output is how a child talks to its parent. You declare it with @Event on an accessor of the child, and it becomes an Output whose emit dispatches a CustomEvent on the element of the child. The parent listens to it in its template, like to a native event.

declaringAndEmitting.title: Declaring and emitting
declaringAndEmitting.p1: The event is named after the accessor, and the type argument of Output is the type of its detail. Without a type argument the event carries no detail, and emit takes at most the options. The options passed to the decorator apply to every emission; those passed to emit are merged over them for that emission only.

listeningInTheParent.title: Listening in the parent
listeningInTheParent.p1: The parent binds a method to the event with (valueChange)="setQuantity($event)". $event is the CustomEvent itself: the method reads the value in event.detail.
listeningInTheParent.p2: The picker never changes the quantity: it shows its input and asks for a new value with valueChange. The parent owns the quantity and decides: past 5 it ignores the request, and the picker keeps showing the value it receives. Together, an input and an output make a component controlled by its parent, which is how Xaendar replaces two-way binding. cleared has no detail, and its handler takes no argument: a template passes $event only to the events that carry a detail.

eventOptions.title: Event options
eventOptions.p1: By default the event is dispatched on the element of the child and goes no further: only the listeners on that element receive it. bubbles lets it climb through the ancestors, but only within the shadow root containing the child; composed lets it cross shadow roots, up to the document. cancelable lets a listener call preventDefault(): see the edge cases.
eventOptions.p2: Press the four buttons. The template binding on the tag receives everything. bubbling reaches the frame, which is in the same shadow root as the child, but stops at the root, so the host of the parent never sees it. Only escaping, and plain with the options overridden, reach the host and the document. On the way out the target is retargeted: the document sees the outermost component containing the source, while composedPath()[0] is still the element that emitted it.
eventOptions.p3: The frame, the host and the document listen with addEventListener: a template can only bind a custom event on the tag of the component that declares it. Listeners added outside the template are yours to remove, which the example does in onDestroy.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.example1: Events emitted while the child is mounted
edgeCases.p1: The parent attaches its listeners before inserting the child, so every event of the child arrives: the ones emitted from onInit and afterRender, and the one emitted from onDestroy, since the listeners are still in place while the child is removed.
edgeCases.example2: A detail that looks like options
edgeCases.p2: emit takes its only argument for the options only when it is an instance of EventOptions. Any other value is the detail, even an object holding the keys bubbles, cancelable or composed: the booking arrives whole in event.detail, and its cancelable does not change the event.
edgeCases.p3: emit returns nothing, so the child cannot know whether a listener called preventDefault(). To make a cancelable event useful, declare it with @Event, so that templates can listen to it, and dispatch it yourself with dispatchEvent, which returns false when the event was canceled. Listeners run synchronously, so the result is ready on the next line. The event carries the mode of the note as its detail.

callout2.heading: Event names are case-sensitive
callout2.p1: The name of the event is the name of the accessor, letter by letter. HTML attributes are case-insensitive, but event bindings are not: (valuechange) does not match valueChange.

callout3.heading: Custom events on native elements
callout3.p1: On a native element a template can only bind the events of HTMLElementEventMap, so it cannot catch a bubbling custom event on an ancestor of the child. Add the listener with addEventListener, as the frame does in the second example.

callout4.heading: Native events on a component tag
callout4.p1: An event the component does not declare is a native event of its element: (click) on a component tag compiles, with $event typed through HTMLElementEventMap, and a name that is neither an output nor a native event fails the build. The listener receives only the events that reach the tag: native events that are composed, like click, leave the shadow root of the component, while the others, like change, stay inside it.

callout6.heading: Names already taken by HTMLElement
callout6.p1: A component is an HTMLElement, so an event named remove, click or focus would replace a method of the element. TypeScript rejects it, and so it does for an input or a signal named title, lang or hidden. Choose another name, or keep the name in templates with an alias.

summary.td6: Listens in the template of the parent. $event is the CustomEvent.

hostBindings.title: Host bindings with @HostProperty and @HostEvent
hostBindings.lead: A component is an element of the page: the template using it can set its attributes and listen to its events. Some of them, though, belong to the component, whoever uses it: the role of a switch and its state for assistive technologies, a class its stylesheet reads with :host(.on), the clicks and the keys that operate it. @HostProperty and @HostEvent declare them on the members of the class, and keep them on the host element.

attributesAndClasses.title: Attributes and classes
attributesAndClasses.p1: @HostProperty('name') on a field, a getter or an accessor writes its value in the attribute name of the host element; @HostProperty('class.name') toggles the class name, which the element has while the value is truthy. The member is read inside an effect: a value that reads no signal is written once, while a signal, or a getter reading signals, is written again each time they change.
attributesAndClasses.example1: A switch drawn by its own element
attributesAndClasses.p2: Click the switches, or reach them with Tab and press Space. role reads no signal and is written once. on holds a signal, and the host has the class on while it is true: the stylesheet draws the switch from :host(.on). The getters of aria-checked, aria-disabled and tabindex are written again when on or locked change. locked is an input reflected on the host: the parent binds it, and the stylesheet reads :host([locked]). Inspect the Wi-Fi switch with the developer tools to watch its attributes change while you turn the airplane mode on.

events.title: Events of the host
events.p1: @HostEvent('name') on a method listens to the event on the host element, from the connection to the disconnection. The method receives the event, typed by its parameter, or takes no parameter at all. In the switch, the clicks call toggle, those on the projected label included, and onKeydown turns Space and Enter into a toggle. The options are the ones of addEventListener: capture, once and passive.
events.p2: The listener hears the native events of the host, the events dispatched on it, the outputs of the component included, and the events bubbling from its content. From its shadow root only the composed events come out, such as click and keydown: change and the outputs of the children stay inside, and are listened to in the template. See HostEvent.

values.title: From values to attributes
values.p1: null, undefined and false remove the attribute, true writes it empty, and any other value is written as a string. That suits boolean attributes such as hidden, but not ARIA states, which need the text false: return String(value) for them, as the switch does for aria-checked.

timing.title: When they are applied
timing.p1: In a component, the attributes, the classes and the listeners are applied after the render and after the queries are updated, right before afterRender: a getter can read a query, and afterRender finds the host ready, while onInit does not. The changes of the signals are written a microtask later, as in every effect.
timing.p2: At disconnection everything is undone: the attributes are removed, the classes taken away, the listeners removed. A component moved in the document loses them, and gets them back at the new connection.

directives.title: In custom directives
directives.p1: A custom directive declares them the same way, and binds the element it is applied to: the bindings start right after its onInit and stop when it is destroyed. The directive below copies a text when its element is clicked, with no onInit and no onDestroy. A structural directive holds no element: TypeScript rejects both decorators there. See Custom directives.

callout1.heading: A member is reactive only through its signals
callout1.p1: The effect sees only the signals the member reads while it runs: a getter returning the length of a plain array, or a field later assigned another plain value, is never written again. Keep the state the host shows in signals.

callout2.heading: false removes the attribute
callout2.p1: aria-checked, aria-expanded and the other ARIA states read the text false, which false would remove: return String(value). To a screen reader a missing aria-checked does not mean unchecked.

callout3.heading: The parent binds the same attribute
callout3.p1: The host is also a tag in the template of the parent, which can write the same attribute, as can a directive applied to the element. The values are not merged: the last write wins. A static attribute of the parent is overwritten at connection, and removed at disconnection. Leave each attribute to a single owner, or take the value of the parent through an input reflected with @HostProperty, as locked does. Classes do not clash: class.name toggles only its own class, and keeps it when the parent writes class.

callout4.heading: Nothing is bound yet in onInit
callout4.p1: The bindings of a component start after the render: in onInit the host has none of its attributes, and the events dispatched there do not reach the @HostEvent methods. The listeners of the parent template, added before the element is inserted, run before them for the same event.

callout5.heading: Errors
callout5.p1: TypeScript rejects the decorators on a structural directive, and @HostEvent on a method with more than one parameter. An empty name, class. alone and a static member throw when the class is defined.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: Writes the value of a field, a getter or an accessor in an attribute of the host: removed for null, undefined and false, empty for true.
summary.td2: Toggles a class of the host while the value is truthy.
summary.td3: Listens to an event of the host with a method, which receives the event.

queries.title: View queries
queries.lead: A view query finds elements in the template of the component and keeps the result in a signal. It is the way to reach the DOM from the class: to focus a field, to measure an element, or to call a method of a child component. The result follows the template: when an @if or an @for adds or removes elements, the query is updated.

queryingTheTemplate.title: Querying the template
queryingTheTemplate.p1: @Query holds the first element matching a CSS selector, or null. @Query.all holds all of them, in document order. Instead of a selector you can pass the class of a component: the query uses its selector, and the result is typed as an instance of the class, with its public members.
queryingTheTemplate.example1: A query by tag, one by class and one for all the rows
queryingTheTemplate.p2: Add reads the value of the field and empties it through the element found by field, and calls increment() on the badge found by its class. The list is rendered by an @for, and rows follows it: found, a computed signal reading the query, updates by itself.
queryingTheTemplate.p3: A query looks into the shadow root of its component, and only there: it finds the elements the template projects into a child component, since they are written in this template, but not the elements inside the shadow root of the child.

refsAndDirectives.title: Element refs and directives
refsAndDirectives.p1: @Query.ref('name') holds the element an element ref of the template names, #name, and @Query.ref.all the elements of every row of the @for declaring it. Unlike a selector, a ref doesn't depend on the tag or the classes of the element. @Query.ref.required throws when no element is named by the ref.
refsAndDirectives.p2: The class of a custom directive finds the directive, not the element: the query holds the instances applied to the elements of the template, with @@selector or as host directives of a component, typed by the class.
refsAndDirectives.example1: A ref for the field, one for every row, and the directives applied to the rows
refsAndDirectives.p3: Add reads the field through its ref. Mark every row calls a method of each directive found by @Query.all(MarkDirective), and the count follows the signals of the directives.
refsAndDirectives.p4: The queries holding a single element take a read option, which tells what they hold for the element they find: the instance of a directive applied to it, by its class, or the element itself, 'element', also when the target is a directive. The .all variants do not take it.

whenTheResultIs.title: When the result is there
whenTheResultIs.p1: The query is filled right after the render, before afterRender, and it is updated by a MutationObserver each time the elements of the template are added or removed. So it is empty in onInit, and it lags a little behind the changes of the template.
whenTheResultIs.example1: The query before and after the render, and after a change
whenTheResultIs.p2: The template is updated in a microtask after the signal changes, and the query a microtask after that. Read queries in afterRender, in event handlers, or reactively in a computed signal or an effect: an effect created in onInit runs again when the query is filled.

requiredQueries.title: Required queries
requiredQueries.p1: @Query.required is @Query for an element that is always there: its type has no null, and reading the signal throws when no element matches the target. The error names the selector and the component.
requiredQueries.p2: The rules of the previous section still hold: the result is there only after the render, so reading the query in onInit, in an effect created before the render or in the template throws. Read it in afterRender, in event handlers, or in a computed signal read from them. An element inside an @if is not always there: keep @Query for it.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.example1: A query on a class that changes
edgeCases.p1: The observer watches elements being added and removed, not their attributes. Selecting a task changes only its class, so the query on .selected keeps its old result until the list itself changes: add a task and it catches up. Use queries to find elements, and keep the state in signals.

callout3.heading: A class that is neither a component nor a directive
callout3.p1: A class passed to a query must be decorated with @WebComponent, which gives it its selector, or extend CustomDirective. Otherwise the query throws when the component is created, also for a subclass of a component that is not decorated itself: the selector of its parent is not inherited.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: The first element of the template matching target, or null.
summary.td2: All the matching elements, in document order. Notifies only when the list changes.
summary.td3: Like @Query, without null: reading it throws when no element matches.
summary.td4: A CSS selector, the class of a component or the class of a custom directive.
summary.td6: The elements named by the element ref #name, with .all and .required too.
summary.td7: What a single-element query holds for the element: 'element', or the class of a directive applied to it. Not on .all.

registration.title: Selectors and registration
registration.lead: @WebComponent registers the class in the custom elements registry of the browser, under its selector, as soon as the module declaring it is evaluated. From then on every element with that tag name, already in the page or created later, is an instance of the class.

choosingASelector.title: Choosing a selector
choosingASelector.p1: The selector is a custom element name, and the browser is strict about it: it must start with a lowercase letter, contain a hyphen, contain no uppercase letters, and not be one of the few reserved names such as font-face. A prefix shared by the whole application (app-, acme-) keeps the names readable and avoids clashes with third-party elements.
choosingASelector.example1: customElements.define with valid and invalid names
choosingASelector.p2: The compiler applies the same rules at build time, and stops before the browser would:

oneNameOneClass.title: One name, one class
oneNameOneClass.p1: A name can be defined only once, and a class can be defined under one name only: the example above shows both errors. The compiler checks every component of the project, so two classes claiming the same selector fail the build; without that check, the second define would throw at run time.

usingAComponentIn.title: Using a component in a template
usingAComponentIn.p1: A template uses a component in two separate steps.
usingAComponentIn.li1: At build time, the template imports the class with @import. The compiler reads the class to learn its selector, its inputs and its outputs, and type-checks the bindings against them.
usingAComponentIn.li2: At run time, the module declaring the class must have been evaluated, so that the decorator has defined the element. The template does it: its module imports the modules it imports with @import, so a component is defined before the template using it is rendered, and the bundler can split the site along the templates. Only bootstrap.ts, loaded by the entry point once the signals are installed, imports the root component:
usingAComponentIn.p2: A tag with a hyphen that the template neither imports nor declares as a custom element of another library (see below) fails the build:

customElementsOfOther.title: Custom elements of other libraries
customElementsOfOther.p1: A template can also use the custom elements of other libraries, such as Shoelace or an element written without Xaendar. Their tags are declared in customElements, in xaendar.json, as a list of patterns where * stands for any sequence of characters. A project driving Vite directly passes the same list to the plugin: xaendarPlugin({ customElements: ['sl-*'] }).
customElementsOfOther.example1: An element written without Xaendar, used in a template
customElementsOfOther.p2: The compiler treats these tags like native elements. A binding writes an attribute, so the element receives a string: here the stars read count from their attribute. A value that is not a string, such as an object, goes to a property in code, as shown in Using DOM APIs. $event gets the type HTMLElementEventMap declares for the event, and is any for an event it does not declare, such as the vanilla-change of the stars. The library still has to define the element at run time: the example imports its module.

loadingAComponentOn.title: Loading a component on demand
loadingAComponentOn.p1: A template loads the modules it imports with @import. When a component has to arrive later, @import lazy gives the compiler the class to type-check against, without loading the module: something else loads it on demand, with a dynamic import(), and the component is defined only when its module arrives. The elements with its tag that are already in the page are then upgraded: the browser runs the constructor on them and connects them, but the bindings applied to them in the meantime did not reach any input, because there was no input yet: they were written as plain attributes, which components do not read.
loadingAComponentOn.example1: Bindings applied before and after the definition
loadingAComponentOn.p2: Click count + 1 first, then load the panel. The first panel shows the default values: its static label will never arrive, and its count only arrives with the next change, since a reactive binding writes the input when its value changes. The second panel is rendered by an @if only after the module has been loaded, so it gets every binding. That is the rule: render a lazy component only once customElements.get() knows it, or once the promise of customElements.whenDefined() is resolved.

callout1.heading: An element that is never defined stays empty, silently
callout1.body: A component imported lazy in a template and never loaded compiles, and renders as an empty, undefined element: no shadow root, no content, no error. The :defined pseudo-class can style it while it waits, as the lazy example does.

callout2.heading: A tag both imported and declared
callout2.body: A tag matching a pattern of customElements cannot also be a component imported by the template: the build fails, so that the compiler never treats one of your components as an element of another library. Keep the patterns specific to the other libraries.

callout3.heading: The registry is global
callout3.body: There is one registry per page and no way to undefine a name. Two applications on the same page, or two versions of the same library, cannot define the same selector: the prefix is the only protection.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: @import { Class } from "./path.xd.component.ts"
summary.td2: In a template: makes a component known to the compiler. Build time only.
summary.td3: customElements.get(name)
summary.td4: The class defined with that name, or undefined.
summary.td6: A promise resolved when the name gets defined.
summary.td7: CSS pseudo-classes matching defined and not yet defined elements.
summary.td9: In xaendar.json: the tags of other libraries that templates use like native elements. Build time only.

styling.title: Styling
styling.lead: Each component has its own stylesheet, adopted by its shadow root: its rules match the elements of its template and nothing else, and the rules of the page do not match them. What crosses the boundary is decided by CSS itself: inherited properties, custom properties, the host element, the projected content and the parts a component exposes.

theComponentStylesheet.title: The component stylesheet
theComponentStylesheet.p1: styleUrl points to a .css file, or to a Sass or Less one, as described below. The plugin compiles it once into a CSSStyleSheet, which every instance of the component adopts when it is connected: a hundred instances share one stylesheet. Components pointing to the same file share it too.
theComponentStylesheet.example1: Two paragraphs with the same class
theComponentStylesheet.p2: Both paragraphs have the class title, and each stylesheet styles only its own: the red border stays in the parent, the uppercase stays in the child. The color and the italic, instead, reach the child: they are set on its host element, and inherited properties flow into the shadow root like into any other element.

stylingTheHost.title: Styling the host
stylingTheHost.p1: Inside the stylesheet, :host matches the element of the component itself. A custom element is display: inline by default, so most components set a display here. :host(selector) matches the host only when it also matches the selector: a class, an attribute or a state set from outside.
stylingTheHost.p2: The parent only sets a class and an attribute; the chip decides how they look. Each chip listens to its own (click): a native event bound on the tag of a component is added to its element, as on a native element. See the edge cases of Outputs. A component can also set classes and attributes on its own host, with @HostProperty: see Host bindings.

themingWithCustomProperties.title: Theming with custom properties
themingWithCustomProperties.p1: Custom properties are inherited, so they cross shadow roots: a component can read var(--accent, fallback) and let any ancestor decide the value. This is the way to offer a theming API without exposing the internals.
themingWithCustomProperties.example1: An accent color and a radius set on a container

partsAndProjectedContent.title: Parts and projected content
partsAndProjectedContent.p1: An element with a part attribute can be styled from outside with ::part(name), and only that element: its children stay private. The content projected into a slot belongs to the template that wrote it, so it is styled by that template’s stylesheet; the component can add rules for it with ::slotted(selector), which only matches the elements assigned to a slot, not their descendants.
partsAndProjectedContent.p2: When both stylesheets style the same projected element, the outer one wins: the green of the parent beats the red of ::slotted(.note). A component’s ::slotted rules are defaults that the user of the component can override.

dynamicClassesAndStyles.title: Dynamic classes and styles
dynamicClassesAndStyles.p1: class and style are attributes like any other: bind them to an expression and the attribute is rewritten when the value changes. Building the string in a computed signal keeps the template short and the binding reactive. A single class that comes and goes is shorter with [class.name]="{ condition }", as the label does: see Binding.

sassAndLess.title: Sass and Less
sassAndLess.p1: A .scss or .sass file (the indented syntax) is compiled with the sass package, a .less file with less. Imports between stylesheets work: @use, @forward and @import in Sass, @import in Less are resolved at build time, relative to the stylesheet, and the dev server watches every imported file, partials included. The resulting CSS then goes through the same steps as a .css file.
sassAndLess.p2: The two packages are optional peer dependencies of @xaendar/build-tools: the project installs the one it uses, with npm i -D sass or npm i -D less. xd new adds it to package.json when you choose one of these formats. Without it, the first stylesheet that needs it fails to compile:
sassAndLess.p3: An error in the Sass or Less code is reported in the same way: Failed to compile style, the path of the stylesheet, then the message of the compiler.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: A binding on a native element sets an attribute, and an attribute is a string: an object becomes [object Object], and the browser ignores it. Build the string yourself.

callout2.heading: Other preprocessors
callout2.p1: Only .css, .scss, .sass and .less files are supported: Stylus and the others are rejected.

callout3.heading: @import and relative URLs in a component stylesheet
callout3.p1: The stylesheet is built in the browser from the text of the file, so it has no URL of its own. In a .css file, an @import rule is dropped with a warning: only the imports of Sass and Less, resolved at build time, work. A relative url() is resolved against the page instead of the stylesheet, whatever its format. Use one file per component, or share a file between components, and refer to assets with absolute paths, for example from the public folder.

callout4.heading: The global stylesheet does not reach components
callout4.body: The styles of the page, including resets such as box-sizing: border-box, do not apply inside shadow roots. Repeat them in the component stylesheets, or share a stylesheet file between components.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: :host, :host(selector)
summary.td2: the component
summary.td3: The host element, optionally only when it matches the selector.
summary.td4: ::slotted(selector)
summary.td6: The elements assigned to its slots, not their descendants.
summary.td9: The element with part="name" inside the component.
summary.td12: A custom property set by any ancestor.
summary.td14: Custom elements whose definition is loaded.

conditional.title: Conditional directives
conditional.lead: Directives can be applied by an @if or a @switch written inside a tag, like the other conditional bindings. The element stays; the directive is created when its branch is taken, and destroyed when it is left.

customDirectives.title: Custom directives
customDirectives.example1: A directive applied by a condition
customDirectives.p1: Remove the directive from the first paragraph: onDestroy runs, and the effects of the instance are disposed. Apply it again: a new instance is created, with its own onInit. Nothing survives between the two, so a directive applied conditionally should leave the element as it found it, as this one does with the background.
customDirectives.p2: The second paragraph keeps its directive, and switches only the binding of its input. The instance stays the same, and its effect simply runs again with the new value.

structuralDirectives.title: Structural directives
structuralDirectives.example1: A structural directive added by a condition
structuralDirectives.p1: The paragraph always has exIsEven, and exPositive only while the box is checked. The rule does not change: the element is rendered while every directive currently applied returns true. Check the box while value is negative and even: exPositive joins and the paragraph disappears; uncheck it and the paragraph comes back. Both directives are defined in Structural directives.

callout1.heading: Conditional inputs only on custom directives
callout1.p1: A custom directive can bind its inputs inside a condition, as the second paragraph above does. A structural directive cannot: apply the whole directive conditionally instead, one per branch.

callout2.heading: No directives inside a directive
callout2.p1: The parentheses of a directive hold its inputs and listeners, and conditions over them, but no other directive.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: A new instance each time the branch is taken; onDestroy when it is left.
summary.td2: Same instance; only the binding of the input changes.
summary.td3: The directive joins or leaves the AND of the structural directives of the element.
summary.td4: Not allowed.

custom.title: Custom directives
custom.lead: A custom directive extends CustomDirective and works on the element it is applied to: it listens to it, changes it, measures it, or puts something next to it. The same behavior can then be added to any element of any template with @@name, without a wrapper component.

theElementTheInputs.title: The element, the inputs and the hooks
theElementTheInputs.p1: The element is in this.element, typed by the argument of CustomDirective. The inputs are declared with @Property and read as signals, so this.effect keeps the text of the tooltip in sync: hover Save, click it, and the tooltip changes while it is shown.
theElementTheInputs.p2: onInit runs when the directive starts, onDestroy when the element leaves the template. The effects created with this.effect are disposed on their own, right after onDestroy; the rest has to be undone by hand. This directive appends its tooltip to the body, outside the element, so it removes it in onDestroy: otherwise a tooltip shown while its element is removed would stay on the page.

outputs.title: Outputs
outputs.p1: A directive declares outputs with @Event, like a component. It has no element of its own: its events are dispatched on the element it is applied to, and the template listens to them inside the parentheses of the directive.
outputs.example1: Closing a menu with a click outside
outputs.p2: The directive listens to the whole document, and emits outside when the pointer is pressed out of its element. The check uses composedPath() instead of target: the page is made of shadow roots, and the target of an event seen from the document is the outermost host, never the element inside it.
outputs.p3: Here the output carries a detail, and $event is the CustomEvent with the size.
outputs.p4: The parentheses also accept native events: they are added to the element as if they were written on the tag.

hostBindings.title: Binding the element
hostBindings.p1: @HostProperty and @HostEvent work in a directive as in a component, on the element it is applied to: the attributes are written and the listeners added right after onInit, and everything is undone when the directive is destroyed. This directive copies a text when its element is clicked, with no onInit and no onDestroy:
hostBindings.p2: The values, the timing and the edge cases are described in Host bindings.

svgElements.title: SVG elements
svgElements.p1: The argument of CustomDirective can be any element type. A directive meant for SVG circles gets the SVG API of the circle, such as its animated radius, without casts.

generics.title: Generic directives
generics.p1: A directive class can have type parameters. The template gives them as type arguments right after the selector, between < and >: the types of the inputs and of the outputs of the directive are checked against them.
generics.p2: The type arguments follow the order of the type parameters. Without type arguments, the type parameters are inferred from the values bound to the inputs, as TypeScript does for a function call (items="{ rows() }" gives Item the type of the rows), and the ones nothing is inferred for take their default type (Key = string), or any when they have none. With type arguments nothing is inferred, as for a call too: the ones left out take their default type, and leaving out one without a default type is an error. A constraint of the type parameter is checked on the argument. Type arguments are only for the type-check: they have no effect at runtime. A structural directive takes them the same way: *each<Item>(…).

hostDirectives.title: Host directives
hostDirectives.p1: A component can apply custom directives to its own element, without anyone writing them in a template: they are listed in the hostDirectives option of @WebComponent. Each entry is the class of a directive, or an object with the class (directive) and the properties and events of the directive the component exposes.
hostDirectives.p2: An exposed input is bound by the templates using the component as if it were its own (hint="…"), and an exposed output is dispatched on the component, so they listen to it with (shown)="…". Each entry of properties and events is a name, exposed as it is, or an object with the name and the alias to expose it with: { name: 'text', alias: 'hint' } exposes the input text as hint. What is not listed stays private to the directive: its events are not dispatched on the component at all. The metadata of the exposed inputs and outputs are read from the class of the directive, so they are type-checked and suggested like the ones of the component.
hostDirectives.p3: The instances are in hostDirectives, a map keyed by the class of the directive: this.hostDirectives.get(TooltipDirective) is typed as the directive, so the component reads its inputs and calls its methods. A template cannot name a class: keep the instance in a field of the component, and the template reads it from there.
hostDirectives.p4: The directives start before onInit of the component, which finds them ready, and stop after its onDestroy, with their effects disposed. A directive can be listed once, and an exposed input cannot have the name of an input of the component or of another host directive: both are errors raised when the element is created.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.example1: What a directive sees in onInit
edgeCases.p1: A directive starts once the element has its attributes and is in the document, but before its children are rendered: onInit sees the id and the bound label, yet no list item, and the items appear a microtask later. Code that needs the children can wait for a microtask, or watch them with a MutationObserver.
edgeCases.p2: A directive receives its inputs before onInit: the label is already first, not the default. So does a child component, as shown in Inputs.

callout1.heading: The element is not there in the constructor
callout1.p1: The element of the directive is set after the constructor: there, this.element is undefined, and the inputs still hold their defaults. this.effect can be called there, as in a component: the effect runs at once and is disposed with the directive. The setup reading the element or the inputs belongs in onInit.

callout2.heading: Once per element, and only known inputs
callout2.p1: A directive can be applied once to the same element. Its inputs are checked like those of a component: unknown names and wrong types are compile errors.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: The element the directive is applied to, available from onInit.
summary.td2: Runs once the inputs are bound and the element is in the document, before its children are rendered.
summary.td3: Runs when the element leaves the template, before the effects are disposed.
summary.td4: An effect disposed with the directive; returns a function disposing it earlier.
summary.td5: Dispatches an event on the element; used by the outputs.
summary.td6: Inputs and outputs, as in components.
summary.td7: Bind attributes, classes and listeners of the element, from onInit to the destruction.

overview.title: Directives
overview.lead: A directive adds behavior to an element that a template renders, without wrapping it in a component. Xaendar has two kinds: custom directives, written @@name, act on an element that exists; and structural directives, written *name, decide whether the element exists at all.

twoKindsOfDirectives.title: Two kinds of directives
twoKindsOfDirectives.example1: A custom and a structural directive
twoKindsOfDirectives.p1: exTint extends CustomDirective: it receives the element it is applied to in this.element, and an effect keeps its background in sync with the color input. exVisibleWhen extends StructuralDirective: it has no element, only a shouldRender() method, and the paragraph exists while the method returns true. Both declare their inputs with @Property, exactly like components.
twoKindsOfDirectives.td7: None: the element may not exist

syntax.title: Syntax
syntax.p1: The inputs and the listeners of a directive go between the parentheses after its name, with the same syntax as the attributes and the listeners of a tag. Without inputs, the parentheses can be left out. An element can have several directives of both kinds.
syntax.p2: Custom directives are covered in Custom directives, structural ones in Structural directives, and directives applied by an @if inside a tag in Conditional directives.

declaringAndRegistering.title: Declaring and registering
declaringAndRegistering.p1: @Directive takes a selector and registers the class under it as soon as the module is evaluated. As for components, a directive has to be known twice: the template imports it with @import, so that the compiler can check its inputs and outputs, and the module is loaded at runtime by the template, before it is rendered.

callout1.heading: Prefix your selectors
callout1.body: Selectors of directives live in a single registry, shared by the whole application and by the libraries it uses. Unlike the names of custom elements, they need no dash: a short prefix, such as ex in these pages, avoids clashes.

callout1.heading: A directive not imported by the template
callout1.p1: The compiler only knows the directives imported by the template, and rejects the others, even when they are registered at runtime.

callout2.heading: A directive not loaded at runtime
callout2.p1: The opposite case compiles: the template imports the class, but no code loads its module before the template is rendered. The decorator never runs: the element using the directive stays empty, and nothing after it in the template is rendered.

callout3.heading: Two directives with the same selector
callout3.p1: The registry accepts a selector once. The compiler reports the clash as soon as it has met both directives, while compiling the templates importing them; at runtime, the second decorator throws when its module is evaluated, even if no template uses it.

callout4.heading: The wrong prefix
callout4.p1: The compiler does not check that @@ is used for custom directives and * for structural ones. The mistake shows up when the element is rendered.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: @Directive({ selector: 'name' })
summary.td2: Registers the class under the selector.
summary.td3: Base class of directives acting on an element of type T.
summary.td4: Base class of directives deciding whether an element is rendered.

structural.title: Structural directives
structural.lead: A structural directive extends StructuralDirective and implements one method, shouldRender(). The element it is applied to, with everything inside it, exists while the method returns true. It is an @if with a name, inputs and logic of its own, reusable in any template.

shouldrender.title: shouldRender
shouldrender.example1: Even numbers, and even positive numbers
shouldrender.p1: shouldRender runs inside an effect: it is evaluated again whenever a signal it reads changes, here the value input. When the outcome becomes true the element is rendered; when it becomes false the element and its subtree are destroyed.
shouldrender.p2: The second paragraph has two structural directives: it is rendered only while all of them return true. The order does not matter, and there is no limit on their number.
shouldrender.p3: Type something in the field, then press +2: the outcome stays true, so the element is left alone and keeps the text. Press +1 and then +1 again: the element is destroyed and created anew, with an empty field. The same happens with @if, as shown in @if.

inputs.title: Inputs
inputs.p1: A structural directive can have any number of inputs, declared with @Property. Since min is a number, it is bound with an expression, min="{ 3 }": a static value would be a string, and the compiler would reject it.

readingOtherSignals.title: Reading other signals
readingOtherSignals.p1: shouldRender tracks every signal it reads, not only the inputs. A signal kept in a module can make the rendering follow the state of the browser.
readingOtherSignals.p2: The signals are created once per media query and shared by all the instances of the directive. A structural directive has no onInit or onDestroy, so it has nowhere to remove a listener it adds: any resource it needs has to live outside of it, like the map of this module.

asynchronousDirectives.title: Asynchronous directives
asynchronousDirectives.p1: shouldRender can return a promise. The element is rendered or destroyed when the promise settles: until then, it stays as it is.
asynchronousDirectives.example1: A permission checked by a server
asynchronousDirectives.p2: Switch to Guest: the panel stays visible during the check, and disappears when the answer arrives. Then try the third button: the check for the guest is still running when the one for the admin starts. When the first answer arrives, the directive has already been evaluated again, so the outcome is discarded: only the latest evaluation decides, and the panel never flickers.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: Only the signals read before the first await are tracked: after it, the evaluation is no longer running inside the effect. The second directive reads its input after waiting, so switching user does not evaluate it again, and the paragraph stays. Read every input at the top of the method, as the first directive does.

callout1.heading: Before the first answer
callout1.body: An asynchronous directive starts with no outcome: the element is not rendered until the first promise resolves to true. A promise that rejects leaves the previous outcome in place, and its error reaches the console as an unhandled rejection: catch it in the method if a failure should hide the element.

callout2.heading: No listeners and no conditional inputs
callout2.p1: A structural directive has no element to dispatch events on, since the element may not exist, so it accepts no listeners. Its inputs cannot be bound conditionally either; the directive itself can be applied by a condition, as shown in Conditional directives.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: Returns boolean or Promise<boolean>; evaluated again when a signal read before the first await changes.
summary.td2: Inputs, as in components; never bound conditionally.
summary.td3: The element is rendered while every directive returns true.
summary.td4: Pending promise
summary.td5: The element keeps its state; outcomes of older evaluations are discarded.

components.title: Components
components.lead: Components are the building blocks of a Xaendar application. Each one is a standard custom element

definingAComponent.title: Defining a component
definingAComponent.li1: A class extending CustomElement, declared in a file ending with .xd.component.ts;
definingAComponent.li4: Optionally a stylesheet, applied only inside the component through shadow DOM.
definingAComponent.p2: The example below contains two components. ex-user-badge receives data through inputs and talks back through an output; ex-user-profile uses it twice. Open the files tabs to read both.
definingAComponent.example1: A parent and a child component

inputs.title: Inputs
inputs.p1: An input is an accessor decorated with @Property. Its value is a signal: read it by calling it, mySignal(), in the class or in the template. The decorator argument is the default value; @Property.required() marks an input the parent must always bind.
inputs.p2: The parent binds an input like an attribute. name="Ada Lovelace" passes a static string, while online="{ adaOnline() }" passes the value of an expression, and keeps it up to date.

outputs.title: Outputs
outputs.p1: An output is an accessor decorated with @Event, typed Output. Calling emit(value) dispatches a CustomEvent named after the accessor, with the value in its detail. The parent listens to it like to any DOM event: (wave)="onWave($event)".

usingAComponent.title: Using a component
usingAComponent.p1: A template declares the components it uses with @import, so that the compiler can check the bindings against their inputs and outputs. The classes must also be imported by your JavaScript at runtime, so that the custom elements get defined.

callout1.body: Components are real custom elements: once defined, <ex-user-badge> works in any HTML page, in another framework, or created with document.createElement().

signals.title: Reactivity with signals
signals.lead: A signal is a value that notifies whoever reads it when it changes. Signals hold the state of your components, and they are what the compiled templates subscribe to.

threePrimitives.title: Three primitives
threePrimitives.td2: A writable signal: read it with count(), change it with set() or update().
threePrimitives.td4: A read-only signal derived from others, recomputed lazily when they change.
threePrimitives.td6: A function that runs now, and again whenever a signal it read changes.
threePrimitives.td7: Side effects: logging, storage, imperative DOM work.
threePrimitives.example1: A signal, a computed signal and an effect

readingAndWriting.title: Reading and writing
readingAndWriting.p1: A signal is a function: calling it returns its value and, inside a computed signal, an effect or a template binding, registers a dependency. set(value) replaces the value; update(fn) computes the new value from the previous one. Writing a value equal to the current one, by Object.is, notifies nobody.

callout1.body: Signals compare values by identity. Pushing into an array, or changing a property of an object, does not change the signal: always produce a new array or object, as items.update(items => [...items, item]) does.

signalsInTemplates.title: Signals in templates
signalsInTemplates.p1: Templates read signals by calling them, exactly like the class: { celsius() }. The compiler turns each interpolation, binding and control flow block into a binding subscribed to the signals it reads, so a change updates only the affected nodes.

effectsOfAComponent.title: Effects of a component
effectsOfAComponent.p1: this.effect() creates an effect bound to the component: it is disposed automatically when the component leaves the page. Create it in onInit or afterRender.

next.title: Next
next.p1: Continue with dynamic templates, or read the signals guides for every detail and edge case.

templates.title: Dynamic templates
templates.lead: A template is an HTML5 file with a few additions: interpolations, bindings, event listeners and control flow blocks. Expressions are written in TypeScript and can use every public member of the component by name.

theSyntaxAtA.title: The syntax at a glance
theSyntaxAtA.td1: Text interpolation: renders the value of the expression as text.
theSyntaxAtA.td3: A static attribute, or a static string for an input of a component.
theSyntaxAtA.td4: A binding: sets the attribute, or the input, to the value of the expression.
theSyntaxAtA.td5: An event listener calling a method of the component; $event is the event.
theSyntaxAtA.td7: Renders a block for each item.
theSyntaxAtA.td9: Renders the block of the matching case.
theSyntaxAtA.example1: Interpolation, bindings, events and control flow

expressions.title: Expressions
expressions.p1: Expressions refer to the members of the component by their bare name: write items(), not this.items(). They can use literals, operators, calls, ternaries, template literals, optional chaining and the usual browser globals (Math, JSON…), but no assignments, arrow functions or new: logic belongs to the class.

callout1.body: Signals are never unwrapped automatically: { count } renders the signal function itself. Always call it: { count() }.

specialCharacters.title: Special characters
specialCharacters.p1: In the text of a template, { always starts an interpolation, @ always starts a control flow block and < always starts a tag. To write them as text, use a character reference as in HTML, @, or interpolate a string: { '@' }. See Template syntax.

next.p1: Read the next steps, or the templates guides.

home.title: Web Components, compiled to surgical DOM updates
home.lead: Xaendar extends HTML5 with a declarative template language. The compiler analyses every template and wires each element, attribute and text node straight to the signals it reads: no virtual DOM, no component re-renders — a signal change touches only the nodes that depend on it.
home.div1: Get started What is Xaendar? Take the tutorial

whyXaendar.title: Why Xaendar
whyXaendar.div1: Native Web Components Every component is a real custom element with its own shadow root: use it anywhere, with any other framework or none.
whyXaendar.div2: Signals at the core State lives in signals based on the TC39 proposal. Derived values are lazy and cached, effects are batched.
whyXaendar.div3: Compiled, type-checked templates Templates are compiled at build time and type-checked against the component class: mistakes fail the build.
whyXaendar.div4: No virtual DOM The generated code binds each DOM node to the signals it reads. Nothing is diffed, nothing is re-rendered.
whyXaendar.div5: Directives Attach reusable behavior to any element with custom directives, or decide whether it exists with structural ones.
whyXaendar.div6: Reactive queries Query the shadow DOM or the projected content: results are signals that follow every DOM change.
