installation.title: Installation
installation.lead: Create a project with the xd command line tool, or add Xaendar to an existing Vite project by hand. Either way you end up with the same four ingredients: the runtime packages, the decorators transform, the Xaendar Vite plugin and the signals polyfill.

createAProjectWith.title: Create a project with the CLI
createAProjectWith.p1: xd new asks the format of the stylesheets (CSS, SCSS, Sass or Less; CSS in this page), creates the folder, writes the files below and runs npm install. npm start runs xd start, which serves the application on port 4200 and rebuilds it as you edit; npm run build runs xd build, which writes the production bundle in dist.
createAProjectWith.p2: Three files deserve a closer look.
createAProjectWith.p3: The page loads a single module script: main.ts, the entry point.
createAProjectWith.p4: The entry point installs the global Signal object that @xaendar/core needs as soon as it is evaluated, then loads bootstrap.ts with await import(). A static import would not work: the imports of a module are evaluated before its body, so @xaendar/core would be evaluated before loadSignals() runs.
createAProjectWith.p5: A component exists in the browser only after its class has been evaluated: @WebComponent then registers it with customElements.define(). Every component and directive your pages use must be imported, directly or indirectly, by bootstrap.ts.

addXaendarToA.title: Add Xaendar to a project by hand
addXaendarToA.li1: Install the runtime packages and the build tooling.
addXaendarToA.li2: Register the decorators transform and the Xaendar plugin in the Vite configuration, in this order.
addXaendarToA.li3: Configure TypeScript. Xaendar uses standard decorators and the accessor keyword, so do not enable experimentalDecorators. The plugin type-checks the templates with the tsconfig.json found in the directory Vite is started from.
addXaendarToA.li4: Call loadSignals() in your entry point, then load the rest of the application with await import(), as the main.ts above does: @xaendar/core is then evaluated after the polyfill is installed.

yourFirstComponent.title: Your first component
yourFirstComponent.p1: A component is a class extending CustomElement, decorated with @WebComponent, plus a template and an optional stylesheet. The file names matter: the plugin only compiles classes declared in files ending with .xd.component.ts.
yourFirstComponent.p2: Continue with the Essentials for a quick tour, or follow the tutorial to build a small application step by step.

callout1.heading: The polyfill is not loaded
callout1.p1: @xaendar/core reads Signal.subtle while its modules are evaluated. If loadSignals() has not run yet, the application stops before rendering anything:
callout1.p2: Import the modules that use @xaendar/core with await import(), after the call to loadSignals(): the static imports of a module are evaluated before its body, even when they are written after the call.

callout2.heading: A component that is never imported renders nothing
callout2.p1: The @import statement of a template is only read by the compiler, to type-check the bindings. If the class is never imported by your JavaScript, the custom element is never defined: the browser keeps an empty unknown element and reports no error.

callout3.heading: Components must be defined before their parent renders
callout3.p1: If a parent renders while a child it uses is still undefined, the bindings of the child are set as plain string attributes: once the child is defined, its inputs hold their default values until a bound signal changes again. Import the leaf components first, or append the root element only once every module has been imported, as this site does. See Selectors and registration.

callout4.heading: The order of the Vite plugins matters
callout4.p1: The Xaendar plugin injects the template into the static block generated by the decorators transform. If the transform runs after it, the build fails with:

notFound.lead: This page does not exist, or it has moved. Try the search in the top bar, or start again from the home page.

overview.title: What is Xaendar?
overview.lead: Xaendar is a framework for building Web Components declaratively. A component is a TypeScript class plus a template written in an extended HTML5 syntax; the compiler turns the template into code that updates the DOM with the precision of hand-written JavaScript.

fineGrainedReactivityDecided.title: Fine-grained reactivity, decided at build time
fineGrainedReactivityDecided.p1: Most component frameworks run a render function again when the state changes, and compare its output with the previous one: the virtual DOM diff. Xaendar does neither.
fineGrainedReactivityDecided.p2: At build time the compiler analyses each template and finds, for every element, attribute and text node, the expression that produces it. At runtime each expression becomes a tiny reactive binding, subscribed only to the signals it reads. A signal change runs exactly the bindings that depend on it, and each binding writes exactly one node.
fineGrainedReactivityDecided.example1: Only the nodes reading a signal are updated
fineGrainedReactivityDecided.p3: The log comes from a MutationObserver attached to the card. Click the buttons and watch which nodes flash: incrementing touches one text node and one attribute, renaming touches one text node, and the static paragraph never appears.

theBuildingBlocks.title: The building blocks
theBuildingBlocks.td2: A class extending CustomElement and decorated with @WebComponent: a real custom element, rendered in its own shadow root.
theBuildingBlocks.td5: HTML5 extended with interpolation, bindings, events and control flow (@if, @for, @switch), compiled at build time.
theBuildingBlocks.td8: A reactive value: whatever reads it, a template binding, a computed signal or an effect, is notified when it changes.
theBuildingBlocks.td11: Reusable behavior attached to an element (@@name), or a condition deciding whether the element exists at all (*name).
theBuildingBlocks.td14: A signal holding the elements that match a selector, in the shadow DOM or in the projected content.

theLifeOfA.title: The life of a component
theLifeOfA.li1: Build. The Vite plugin reads every *.xd.component.ts file, finds its template and stylesheet, type-checks the template against the class and compiles it into a render function.
theLifeOfA.li2: Definition. Importing the class evaluates @WebComponent, which calls customElements.define().
theLifeOfA.li3: Connection. When the element enters the document its shadow root adopts the stylesheet, onInit runs, the render function builds the DOM and wires the bindings, and afterRender runs last.
theLifeOfA.li4: Updates. A signal change re-runs only the bindings reading it, batched in a microtask.
theLifeOfA.li5: Disconnection. onDestroy runs, then every binding, listener and effect of the component is disposed and its rendered nodes are removed.

thePackages.title: The packages
thePackages.td1: Decorators, base classes and the template runtime. Its @xaendar/core/signals entry exports signal, computed, effect and untracked.
thePackages.td2: The Signal polyfill, based on the TC39 proposal, installed by loadSignals().
thePackages.td3: The template lexer, parser, type checker and code generator.
thePackages.td8: Utilities and types shared by the other packages.

callout1.body: Application code only imports @xaendar/core, @xaendar/core/signals and @xaendar/signals. The other packages are build and editor tooling.

whatXaendarDoesNot.title: What Xaendar does not do
whatXaendarDoesNot.p1: Xaendar is deliberately small. There is no dependency injection, no router, no pipes and no two-way binding: shared state lives in plain modules of signals, formatting lives in methods, and forms are wired with events. The Coming from Angular page maps every Angular concept to its Xaendar counterpart, and the Patterns section shows the idiomatic way to cover the gaps.

asyncData.title: Async data
asyncData.lead: Signals hold values, not promises. Loading data means writing signals when the answer arrives: one for the state of the request, one for the data, one for the error. The template then renders whatever state it finds.

loadingErrorData.title: Loading, error, data
loadingErrorData.p1: load is an ordinary async method. It sets status to loading, awaits the fake server, and writes either the user or the error. An @switch over status picks what to show. Writes after an await are fine: only reads after an await escape tracking, and here nothing reads signals.
loadingErrorData.p2: The request is tied to an AbortController: a new request aborts the one in progress, and so does onDestroy, so that no answer arrives for a component that is gone.

requestsThatOvertakeEach.title: Requests that overtake each other
requestsThatOvertakeEach.example1: The last answer, or the last request
requestsThatOvertakeEach.p1: User 1 is slow and user 2 is fast. The naive loader writes every answer in the order it arrives, so it ends up showing user 1, which was asked for first. The other loader aborts the stale request, and shows user 2. When an API cannot be aborted, the same result comes from a counter: each request remembers its number, and an answer is written only if no newer request was sent.

loadingWhenAnInput.title: Loading when an input changes
loadingWhenAnInput.p1: A component loading data for one of its inputs can start the request from an effect, which runs again whenever the input changes. The request itself runs in untracked, so that whatever it reads does not become a dependency of the effect.

callout2.heading: Reading signals after an await
callout2.body: Code after an await runs outside of the effect that started it, so the signals it reads are not tracked. Read what the request depends on before the first await. The same rule applies to asynchronous structural directives.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: State of the request
summary.td2: A signal such as 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error' | 'ready', rendered by @switch
summary.td3: Stale answers
summary.td4: AbortController, or a request counter
summary.td6: this.effect reading the inputs, the request in untracked

forms.title: Forms
forms.lead: Xaendar has no form module and no two-way binding. A form is made of plain elements: their events write signals, computed signals validate them, and a directive writes values back into the fields when the state has to drive them.

readingTheFields.title: Reading the fields
readingTheFields.p1: Each field has a listener writing its signal: input for text fields, change for selects and checkboxes. The method receives the event and reads value or checked from its target, since $event.target is typed EventTarget | null, which has neither, as explained in Events.
readingTheFields.p2: errors is a computed signal over the fields, so it is always up to date, and the template shows it only after the first attempt to submit. The submit listener calls preventDefault(), which keeps the browser from reloading the page; novalidate turns off the validation of the browser, replaced here by the computed one.

writingTheFields.title: Writing the fields
writingTheFields.p1: Reading is enough as long as the user is the only one changing the fields. When the state changes them too, with a reset, a default or a formatting, binding value is not enough.
writingTheFields.example1: The value attribute and the value property
writingTheFields.p2: Type in the first field, then press Reset: the signal is cleared, the field is not. A binding sets the value attribute, which a field only uses as its initial value: once the user has typed, the field shows its value property, and ignores the attribute. The second field uses exBindValue, a directive writing the property in an effect, and follows the signal in both directions. The same directive drives the select.
writingTheFields.p3: The directive skips the write when the field already holds the value: writing it again while the user types would move the caret to the end.

callout1.heading: A select gets its options after its directives
callout1.body: A custom directive starts before the children of its element are rendered, as shown in Custom directives. A select has no options yet in onInit, so a value written there is lost and the first option stays selected. exBindValue starts its effect a microtask later, when the options exist.

callout2.heading: Checkboxes
callout2.p1: checked is a boolean attribute: bound to false, it still checks the box. And, like value, it is only the initial state.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: Read a field
summary.td2: (input) or (change) calling a method that reads event.target
summary.td3: Validate
summary.td4: A computed over the fields
summary.td8: A directive setting the property in an effect

htmlRendering.title: Rendering HTML
htmlRendering.lead: An interpolation always creates a text node, and a binding on a native element always sets an attribute. A string of HTML therefore shows up as text, which is the safe default. Rendering it as markup takes a directive that sets innerHTML.

aDirectiveForInnerhtml.title: A directive for innerHTML
aDirectiveForInnerhtml.p1: exInnerHtml writes its input into innerHTML from an effect, so the preview follows every keystroke. The Markdown converter escapes the whole source before adding its own tags: the HTML typed in the editor comes out as text, and the only markup in the result is the one the converter writes.
aDirectiveForInnerhtml.p2: The inserted elements live in the shadow root of the component, so its stylesheet styles them: the headings and the code of the preview use the rules of markdown-preview.css.

callout1.heading: Never trust the HTML
callout1.p1: innerHTML runs the event handlers of the markup it receives: an <img> with an onerror attribute is enough to execute code. HTML from users, or from any source you do not control, must be escaped, as the converter does, or sanitized by a library built for it.

callout1.heading: Inserted HTML is not a template
callout1.body: The string is parsed by the browser, not by the compiler: an interpolation inside it is plain text, a listener written as (click) is an ordinary attribute, and no directive is applied. Every change of the input replaces the whole content, so the inserted elements lose their state, such as the focus or a text selection.

callout2.heading: The element must have no other content
callout2.body: The directive replaces whatever the element contains, and the children written in the template are rendered right after onInit, as shown in Custom directives. Apply it to an empty element.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: The string as text, tags included.
summary.td2: The string parsed as HTML, updated when it changes.

lists.title: Lists and CRUD
lists.lead: A list is a signal holding an array, replaced by every change, and rendered by an @for with a stable key. Filters, sorting and totals are computed signals over it. Fields that change often can be signals themselves, so that a change updates one cell instead of a row.

anInventory.title: An inventory
anInventory.p1: items is never mutated: adding, inserting and removing all write a new array, as signals compare values with Object.is, explained in Signals. The @for tracks item().id: when the array changes, the rows of the items still present are kept and moved, and only the new ones are created. Insert an item at random, or sort the list: the existing rows move, untouched.
anInventory.p2: visible filters and sorts the items in a computed signal, and the template only renders it; the original order stays in items. The ids come from a counter and are never reused, so the keys stay unique even after removals.
anInventory.p3: The quantity of each item is a signal of its own. The + and − buttons update it in place: the array does not change, no row is touched, and only the cell and the total, a computed signal reading every quantity, are written.
anInventory.p4: The form is read with FormData and cleared with form.reset(): the field has no bound value, so restoring its initial value empties it, with no directive needed. See Forms for fields driven by the state.

callout2.heading: Keys that repeat
callout2.body: Two items with the same key are told apart only by their order, so the state of their rows can swap when the list changes. Derive keys from a counter or from the ids of the server, never from the position or from a field that users can edit, such as the name.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: Add
summary.td2: Remove
summary.td3: Edit a field
summary.td4: item.quantity.update(n => n + 1), with the field as a signal

routing.title: Routing
routing.lead: Xaendar has no router, and a small one takes a few dozen lines: a signal holding the path, a computed signal matching it against the routes, and an @switch rendering the page of the route. This site is built that way.

aRouterInA.title: A router in a module
aRouterInA.example1: Pages, parameters and a back button
aRouterInA.p1: router.ts holds the state of the whole application: path, the history of the visited paths, and route, a computed signal matching the path against patterns such as /users/:id. Any component importing the module shares that state, with no injection: see Shared state. The shell imports path, route and canGoBack in its template, and its attributes reading them are reactive.
aRouterInA.p2: The links keep their href, so they still work as links for the browser and for assistive technologies; a click listener calls preventDefault() and navigates instead. The active link gets aria-current through a conditional binding, and the stylesheet uses it.
aRouterInA.p3: The parameter of the user page reaches a component as an input. Going from user 1 to user 2 keeps the same component and changes the input; going to another route destroys it, along with its state.

readingTheUrl.title: Reading the URL
readingTheUrl.p1: The router of the example keeps the path in memory, because this site already uses the address bar. A real router reads it from the URL, so that pages can be bookmarked and the back button of the browser works. With the hash, the change is small:
readingTheUrl.p2: The History API (pushState and popstate) works the same way, but the server must answer every path with the page of the application.

callout2.heading: State that survives navigation
callout2.body: The @switch destroys the page it leaves. State that has to outlive a page, such as a filter or a draft, belongs in a module, like the router itself.

theming.title: Theming
theming.lead: The shadow DOM keeps the selectors of the page out of components, but not inherited properties, and custom properties are inherited. A theme is therefore a set of custom properties declared on an ancestor, which the components read with var().

tokensAndParts.title: Tokens and parts
tokensAndParts.p1: The stage sets data-theme from a signal, and its stylesheet declares a set of tokens for each value. The cards declare no theme at all: they read --card-bg, --card-text and --accent, with a fallback for when no theme is set. The accent comes from a color field, bound straight into a style attribute with a template literal.
tokensAndParts.p2: The second card shows the other way in: its heading is exposed with part="heading", and the parent styles it with ::part(heading). Tokens suit values shared by many components; parts suit the cases where a component lets its users restyle one specific element. Both are described in Styling.

aThemeForThe.title: A theme for the whole application
aThemeForThe.p1: This site keeps the theme in a module signal, writes it on <html data-theme>, and stores the choice. The tokens are declared on :root in the global stylesheet, so every component inherits them.
aThemeForThe.p2: Components render after the scripts of the application are loaded. A small inline script in index.html applies the stored theme, or the one preferred by the system, before the first paint, so the page never flashes in the wrong colors.

callout1.heading: :root inside a component
callout1.p1: A shadow root has no root element, so :root in the stylesheet of a component matches nothing. Tokens local to a component go on :host.

callout2.heading: Only inherited properties cross the boundary
callout2.body: A theme cannot restyle the inside of a component with ordinary selectors. What the component does not read from a custom property, or expose as a part, stays as the component defines it.

api.title: API reference
api.lead: Every symbol exported by the packages of Xaendar, grouped by package. Each one links to its page: what it does, its signature, its options and members one by one, and examples. Filter by name or by kind.

packages.@xaendar/build-tools: The Vite plugin compiling templates and stylesheets, and its options.
packages.@xaendar/common: Utilities shared by the packages: case conversion, object helpers, custom element names.
packages.@xaendar/types: Utility types shared by the packages: constructors, decorators, functions.

comingFromAngular.title: Coming from Angular
comingFromAngular.lead: Xaendar borrows much of its vocabulary from Angular: decorators, signals, a control flow with @if and @for, structural directives. Under the names, the model is different: every component is a real custom element with a shadow root, templates are compiled into direct updates of single nodes, and there is no framework around them: no modules, no injector, no zone.

whatWorksDifferently.title: What works differently
whatWorksDifferently.li2: Bindings set attributes. On native elements a binding calls setAttribute: a value stops mattering once the user types, and disabled="{ false }" still disables. See Binding and Forms.
whatWorksDifferently.li3: A removed element is destroyed. When a template removes an element, its instance is gone, and rendering it again creates a new one. Moving or reattaching elements with the DOM APIs is not supported. See Lifecycle.
whatWorksDifferently.li4: Templates are strict. Listeners call one method, expressions cannot assign or create objects, and a few characters must be escaped. See the cheat sheet.

The Patterns section shows how to cover the common cases with signals and directives.

Errors of the type checker without a phase are the messages of TypeScript, checked against the class of the component. Positions and paths are left out below.

Bugs are behaviors to be fixed; limitations follow from the design; documentation marks texts in the packages that disagree with what the code does.

advanced.title: Advanced: Signal.subtle
advanced.lead: Xaendar signals are a thin layer over the TC39 Signals proposal, polyfilled by @xaendar/signals. The global Signal object exposes the primitives the framework is built on: you rarely need them, but they explain how everything works.

theGlobalSignalObject.title: The global Signal object
theGlobalSignalObject.p1: loadSignals() installs globalThis.Signal once, with Signal.State, Signal.Computed and the Signal.subtle namespace. signal() and computed() wrap a Signal.State and a Signal.Computed in a callable function; effect() combines a Signal.Computed with a Signal.subtle.Watcher.

watchers.title: Watchers
watchers.p1: A Watcher is told, synchronously, that one of the signals it watches may have changed. It cannot do anything in its notify callback — every signal is frozen — except scheduling work. That work reads the pending computed signals with getPending(), then calls watch() to be notified again: a watcher notifies once, then waits to be re-armed.

introspection.title: Introspection
introspection.p1: Signal.subtle can inspect the live graph: introspectSources, introspectSinks, hasSources, hasSinks, and currentComputed, which returns the computed signal being evaluated, if any. Evaluating a computed signal records its sources; once it is watched, the sources record it as a sink too, and unwatching it unlinks it again.

devMode.title: Dev mode
devMode.p1: In dev mode the polyfill logs the errors thrown inside computed signals, watchers and the watched/unwatched callbacks, and warns about invalid state transitions of the graph. loadSignals installs the global object only once, but applies devMode at every call.

callout2.heading: Watching twice throws
callout2.body: watch() on a signal already watched by the same watcher throws Cannot watch a signal that is already being watched; unwatch() on a signal it does not watch throws Cannot unwatch a signal that is not being watched. Both throw while signals are frozen too.

computed.title: Computed signals
computed.lead: computed(fn) creates a read-only signal whose value is derived from other signals. It tracks what fn reads, evaluates lazily and caches the result until a dependency changes.

lazyAndCached.title: Lazy and cached
lazyAndCached.p1: A computed signal does nothing when it is created. The first read runs fn; later reads return the cached value, until one of the signals fn read changes. Even then nothing runs immediately: the value is only marked stale, and recomputed by the next read.
lazyAndCached.p2: While the full name is shown, reading it three times costs nothing and each rename costs one evaluation. Hide it: renames now cost nothing at all, because nobody reads the value. Showing it again evaluates it once.

dynamicDependencies.title: Dynamic dependencies
dynamicDependencies.p1: Dependencies are collected again at every evaluation: a signal read in a branch that was not taken is not a dependency. Here title is only a dependency while showTitle is true.
dynamicDependencies.example1: A dependency that comes and goes

glitchFreeUpdates.title: Glitch-free updates
glitchFreeUpdates.p1: When several computed signals depend on the same source, a change is propagated in topological order: a signal is evaluated only after the signals it depends on, and only once. No consumer ever sees an old value mixed with a new one.
glitchFreeUpdates.example1: A diamond: price → tax, shipping → total

errors.title: Errors
errors.p1: If fn throws, the error is cached like a value: every read throws it again, without running fn, until a dependency changes. The next successful evaluation clears it.
errors.example1: A computed signal that throws on invalid input

optionsAndThis.title: Options and this
optionsAndThis.p1: computed(fn, options) accepts the equals option: when the new result equals the cached one, the consumers are not told that anything changed. Inside a regular function, this is the underlying Signal.Computed; arrow functions keep the this of the class.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.example1: Computed signals reading each other throw

callout2.heading: Keep fn pure
callout2.body: A computed signal can run at unpredictable times — or not at all, if nobody reads it. Do not write signals or perform side effects in fn: use an effect.

callout3.heading: It is read-only
callout3.body: The function returned by computed() has get() but no set() or update(). To change the value, change its dependencies.

summary.td1: computed(fn, options?)
summary.td2: Creates a read-only signal derived from the signals fn reads.
summary.td3: Reads the value, evaluating fn if needed; rethrows a cached error.
summary.td4: options.equals
summary.td5: Decides whether a new result is a change, Object.is by default.

effects.title: Effects
effects.lead: An effect is a function that runs whenever the signals it read change. Effects are how signals reach the outside world: logging, storage, timers, canvas drawing, third-party libraries. Template bindings are effects too.

creatingAnEffect.title: Creating an effect
creatingAnEffect.p1: effect(fn, options?) runs fn immediately and synchronously, recording the signals it reads. When any of them changes, fn runs again — not immediately, but in a microtask. It returns a function that disposes the effect.

batching.title: Batching
batching.p1: All the changes made in the same synchronous block cause a single run, which sees the final values. The run is scheduled as soon as a dependency changes, and happens even if the values end up equal to the ones of the previous run.

effectsOfAComponent.title: Effects of a component
effectsOfAComponent.p1: Components and directives have their own this.effect(fn, options?). It works like effect(), but the effect is disposed automatically when the component leaves the page. Create it in onInit or afterRender; it can also be created in the constructor or in a field initializer, where it runs before the inputs are bound. A standalone effect() lives until its disposer is called, whatever happens to the component that created it.
effectsOfAComponent.p2: Add the child, wait a few seconds and remove it: the effect created with this.effect() stops, the standalone one keeps logging — and keeps the clock ticking — until it is disposed.

options.title: Options
options.li1: onBeforeRun runs before every run, the first one included.
options.li2: onAfterRun runs after every run, even when fn throws.
options.li3: onCleanup runs once, when the effect is disposed.

disposing.title: Disposing
disposing.p1: Calling the disposer stops the effect and releases every subscription. An effect is disposed once: calling the disposer a second time throws, whether the effect is standalone or bound with this.effect(). The disposer of this.effect() also throws after the component or the directive is gone, since the disconnection has already disposed the effect.

errors.title: Errors
errors.p1: An error thrown by the first run is thrown by effect() itself: the effect is removed and no disposer is returned. An error thrown by a later run escapes the microtask: it is not caught by anything, reaches the global error handler, and the effect keeps reacting to the next changes.
errors.example1: Errors on the first run and on later runs

callout1.heading: onCleanup does not run between runs
callout1.body: Unlike the cleanup functions of other libraries, onCleanup runs only when the effect is disposed, not before each re-run. To clean up after each run, do it at the beginning of fn or in onBeforeRun.

callout2.heading: A reverted change still runs the effect
callout2.body: Changing a dependency and changing it back in the same block still schedules a run, as the “a++, a--” button shows. Effects must be idempotent.

callout3.heading: Writing a signal the effect reads loops forever
callout3.p1: Writing signals inside an effect is allowed, but writing one the effect also reads schedules a new run every time: the microtask queue never empties and the page freezes. update() reads without tracking, so it is safe for signals the effect does not otherwise read.

callout5.heading: Documentation mismatches
callout5.body: The JSDoc of onCleanup says it runs before each re-run, and the README of @xaendar/signals shows two synchronous writes producing two runs. Both are wrong: the behavior is the one described on this page.

summary.td1: effect(fn, options?)
summary.td2: Runs fn now and after every change of what it read; returns a disposer.
summary.td3: this.effect(fn, options?)
summary.td4: Same, disposed with the component or directive. Its disposer throws once the effect is disposed.
summary.td8: Called after each run, even a failed one.

options.title: Signal options
options.lead: The second argument of signal() customizes equality and lets a signal know when it starts and stops being observed.

equals.title: equals
equals.p1: Decides whether a new value is a change. See Signals for an example; on computed() it decides whether a new result is a change.

watchedAndUnwatched.title: watched and unwatched
watchedAndUnwatched.p1: watched runs when the signal gains its first live dependent — an effect or a template binding, directly or through computed signals. unwatched runs when it loses the last one. They are the place to start and stop whatever feeds the signal: a timer, a subscription, an event listener.
watchedAndUnwatched.example1: A clock that only ticks while it is displayed

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.example1: Signals are frozen inside watched and unwatched

callout2.heading: Defer the writes
callout2.body: The callbacks run while the reactive graph is being updated, with every signal frozen: reading or writing one throws. Schedule the work instead — queueMicrotask, a timer, an event — as the clock does.

callout4.heading: Inputs have one more option
callout4.body: The @Property decorator accepts these options plus transform and alias. See Inputs.

overview.title: Signals
overview.lead: A signal is a wrapper around a value that notifies its consumers when the value changes. Everything reactive in Xaendar — template bindings, computed signals, effects, queries, component inputs — is built on signals.

creatingAndReadingA.title: Creating and reading a signal
creatingAndReadingA.p1: signal(initialValue, options?), exported by @xaendar/core/signals, creates a writable signal. The signal is a function: call it to read the value. Inside a computed signal, an effect or a template binding, the read also registers a dependency.

writing.title: Writing
writing.li2: update(fn) passes the current value to fn and sets what it returns. The current value is read without tracking, so calling update inside an effect does not make the effect depend on the signal it updates.
writing.p1: A write notifies the consumers synchronously that something changed; the work they do in response — effects and template bindings re-running — is batched and happens in a microtask. See Effects.

equality.title: Equality
equality.p1: Before notifying anybody, a signal compares the new value with the current one. By default it uses Object.is: for objects and arrays that means identity, not content.
equality.example1: Mutating an array in place notifies nobody
equality.p2: push changes the array, but the signal still holds the same reference: nothing re-renders, and the pear stays invisible until a new array is set. Setting the same reference again is ignored too. Treat signal values as immutable and always produce new arrays and objects.
equality.p3: The equals option replaces Object.is. Return true when the new value should be considered the same as the current one: the write is then ignored and the old value is kept.

types.title: Types
types.p1: Signal and Computed are the types of what signal() and computed() return. Annotate component members with them when they hold a signal created somewhere else, for example returned by a function of a shared module: see Sharing state.

callout1.heading: Mutations are invisible
callout1.body: Mutating the value of a signal — push, splice, assigning a property — notifies nobody, and leaves the template showing stale data. The next real change then reveals every hidden mutation at once.

callout2.heading: An equal value is not a change
callout2.body: set and update do nothing when the new value equals the current one. With a custom equals the old value is kept: in the example above, typing “ADA” leaves “Ada” in the signal.

callout3.heading: equals runs inside every write
callout3.body: equals is called synchronously by every set and update, with the current and the new value and with this bound to the underlying Signal.State. Keep it a pure, cheap comparison of its two arguments: if it throws, the write throws.

callout4.heading: Reading outside a reactive context
callout4.body: Reading a signal in an event handler or in a plain method just returns the value: nothing subscribes. Only reads made while a computed signal, an effect or a template binding runs are tracked.

summary.td1: signal(value, options?)
summary.td2: Creates a writable signal.
summary.td3: Reads the value, tracking it in reactive contexts.
summary.td4: sig.set(value)
summary.td5: Replaces the value, unless it is equal to the current one.

sharedState.title: Sharing state
sharedState.lead: Xaendar has no dependency injection. State shared by several components lives in a plain ES module: modules are evaluated once per page, so every component importing one sees the same signals.

aStoreIsA.title: A store is a module
aStoreIsA.p1: Export signals, computed signals and the functions that change them. The two components below know nothing about each other: they only import the same store.
aStoreIsA.p2: Exporting a writable signal lets anyone change it. To keep every change inside the store, keep the signal private and export read-only computed views plus the operations:

exposingSharedSignalsTo.title: Reading shared signals in a template
exposingSharedSignalsTo.p1: A template reads a shared signal by importing it, like any other export of a module: @import { level } from './level.store.ts'. The attribute bindings reading it stay reactive, since the compiler follows the import to the declaration of the signal. A member holding a signal works too, but how you initialize it matters: the compiler decides whether an attribute binding is reactive by looking at the declaration of the members it reads, not at their values.
exposingSharedSignalsTo.example1: The same signal, read three ways
exposingSharedSignalsTo.p2: Raise the level: the three texts follow it, but the second progress bar stays where it was. Text interpolations are always reactive; an attribute binding is reactive only if it names a signal the compiler recognizes — a module signal the template imports, or a member initialized by calling signal() or computed(), annotated with a signal type of @xaendar/core/signals, or initialized with a module variable that is itself a signal. The compiler follows module variables through imports and re-exports to their declaration.

callout1.heading: Signals returned by your own functions freeze attribute bindings
callout1.body: A member like readonly level = readLevel() is evaluated once in attributes: the compiler does not look inside the function. Import the module signal in the template, annotate the member with its signal type, readonly level: Signal<number> = readLevel(), or wrap the call in computed().

callout2.heading: The annotation must be a type of @xaendar/core/signals
callout2.body: The detection is syntactic: it recognizes the names imported from @xaendar/core/signals, and follows module variables to their declarations. A type alias of your own, even if it is the same type, is not recognized.

callout3.heading: One instance per page
callout3.body: Module state is shared by every instance of every component, and survives them: removing all the components does not reset the store. Reset it explicitly when needed, for example between tests.

untracked.title: Reading without tracking
untracked.lead: untracked(fn) runs fn and returns its result, without recording the signals it reads as dependencies of the computation in progress.

whenToUseIt.title: When to use it
whenToUseIt.p1: Use it when an effect or a computed signal needs the current value of a signal, but should not run again when that signal changes. The classic case is context: here the effect sends every new message, signed by the user logged in at that moment — but switching user must not send anything.
whenToUseIt.example1: A tracked and an untracked read

updateIsAlreadyUntracked.title: update() is already untracked
updateIsAlreadyUntracked.p1: sig.update(fn) reads the current value of sig with untracked. That is why an effect can append to a log with update without depending on the log, as several examples on these pages do.

callout1.heading: Only the reads inside fn are untracked
callout1.body: Reads made before or after the call are tracked as usual. And it is the reads that are untracked, not the signals: the same signal read elsewhere in the same effect is still a dependency.

summary.title: Summary
summary.td1: Runs fn without tracking what it reads, and returns its result. Also available as Signal.subtle.untrack.

binding.title: Attribute and property binding
binding.lead: An attribute whose value is an expression in braces is bound: the compiler sets it when the element is created, and again whenever the value changes. On a native element a binding sets an attribute; on the tag of a component it sets the input of the same name.

bindingAttributes.title: Binding attributes
bindingAttributes.example1: Four attributes bound to the same page
bindingAttributes.p1: The whole value has to be one expression: a template literal when you need text around it. The value is converted to a string and written with setAttribute, so class and style are bound like any other attribute, as shown in Styling.

whichExpressionsAreReactive.title: Which expressions are reactive
whichExpressionsAreReactive.p1: Attributes follow a stricter rule than text. The compiler decides at build time whether an attribute can change, by looking for the reactive members the expression names: the signal members, initialized with signal() or computed(), inputs and queries, and the methods and getters of the component whose body reads one of them, a module signal or another reactive method. An attribute that names none is set once.
whichExpressionsAreReactive.example1: Two methods and a computed signal
whichExpressionsAreReactive.p2: percentOf() reads the level in its own body, so its meter follows it. percentFromHelper() reads it through readPercent(), a function outside the class: the compiler does not follow calls it cannot trace back to a signal, so the second meter keeps the value of the first render, while the same method in the text below is reactive, because text interpolations always are. When an attribute needs such a value, declare its reactivity with a computed signal, as percent does. The rule for members that hold a signal created elsewhere is in Shared state.

togglingAClass.title: Toggling a class
togglingAClass.p1: [class.name]="{ expression }" gives the element the class name while the value of the expression is truthy, and takes it away otherwise. The value can be of any type. It works on native elements, on the tags of components, where the class goes on the element itself, and inside conditional bindings, where the class is taken away when its branch is no longer selected. Any class name without spaces follows the dot, [class.is-active] included.
togglingAClass.example1: A bound class attribute and two class bindings
togglingAClass.p2: The class bindings and the class attribute work together, also when it is bound: whenever class is written again, the classes of the bindings are applied on top of it, and a binding whose value is falsy takes its class away even when class lists it. Whether the binding follows its value is decided at build time, as for attributes.

bindingTheInputsOf.title: Binding the inputs of components
bindingTheInputsOf.p1: On the tag of a component the same syntax sets an input, with values of any type, checked against the type of the input. A static value is always a string. See Inputs.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: A boolean attribute counts by its presence, not its value: disabled="false" still disables the button, so the first one is always disabled. Use a conditional binding, which adds and removes the attribute.
edgeCases.example2: The value attribute and the value property
edgeCases.p2: Type in both fields, then reset. A binding sets the value attribute, which is only the initial value of the field: once the user has typed, the field shows its value property, and the first field is not cleared. The second field sets the property from an effect. The Forms pattern wraps this in a directive.

callout1.heading: Text around an expression
callout1.p1: Braces count only when they hold the whole value: a value mixing text and braces is static, and the braces end up in the attribute.

callout2.heading: null and undefined
callout2.body: An attribute bound to null or undefined is not removed: it becomes the text "null" or "undefined". To remove an attribute, bind it conditionally.

callout3.heading: An attribute bound twice
callout3.p1: An attribute can be static or bound, not both, even when one of the two is conditional.

callout4.heading: A boolean attribute without a value
callout4.body: A static disabled written without a value is set to "true": the element is disabled, as expected, but the attribute does not read "" as in HTML.

callout5.heading: A class binding needs an expression
callout5.p1: The value of [class.name] is always an expression in braces: a static value, or no value, does not compile. Brackets only bind classes: [style.color] or [title] are errors too.

callout6.heading: Classes are toggled on the element, not in directives
callout6.body: [class.name] cannot be written in the parentheses of a directive, which only bind its properties: write it on the element. A class can be toggled at most once on an element, as an attribute can be bound once, except in different branches of the same condition.

summary.td1: A static attribute.
summary.td2: An attribute set with String(value), again whenever a signal member it names changes.
summary.td3: The same, with text around the value.
summary.td4: An attribute present only while the condition holds.

summary.td7: The class name, present while the value is truthy.

conditionalBindings.title: Conditional bindings
conditionalBindings.lead: @if and @switch can also appear inside a tag, among its attributes. There they decide which attributes, listeners, inputs and directives the element has: the element itself stays, and only its bindings are added and removed as the conditions change.

attributesAndListeners.title: Attributes and listeners
attributesAndListeners.p1: Lock the task: the button gets disabled and a new title; unlock it and both are replaced by the attributes of the @else branch. Turn editing off: the listener is removed, and clicks are no longer counted. Pick a priority: data-priority is set, changed or removed, and the stylesheet does the rest. Boolean attributes such as disabled are the main use: they count by their presence, so they cannot be bound to false, as explained in Binding.
attributesAndListeners.p2: Conditions are reactive, like those of the blocks, and conditional bindings can be nested. A branch can hold the same things a tag can: static and bound attributes, listeners and directives. The directives applied conditionally have a page of their own: Conditional directives.

inputsOfComponents.title: Inputs of components
inputsOfComponents.p1: On the tag of a component, a conditional binding sets an input while the condition holds. When it stops holding, the input goes back to its default value, not to the last value it received.
inputsOfComponents.example1: An input bound only while linked

callout2.heading: Required inputs in every branch
callout2.p1: A required input bound conditionally must be bound in every branch, including an @else or a @default, or outside the condition.

callout3.heading: An attribute is either static or conditional
callout3.p1: The same attribute cannot be written both outside and inside a condition. Different branches of the same condition, instead, can bind it each in their own way.

events.title: Event listeners
events.lead: An attribute whose name is in parentheses listens to the event of that name and calls a method of the component, of one of its members, such as cart.clear(), or of an element ref, such as dialog.showModal(). The handler is always one call to a method, whose arguments are expressions: the logic lives in the class, where it can be read, typed and tested.

callingAMethod.title: Calling a method
callingAMethod.li2: $event, the event itself, in any position, and its properties, as in $event.key;
callingAMethod.li3: members of the component, variables of an @for and element refs, with their properties, as in color().id or field.value;
callingAMethod.li5: expressions and calls, as in count() + 1 or format(item().id), evaluated when the event fires;
callingAMethod.li4: a signal without the call, which passes the signal itself: bump changes whichever counter it receives.
callingAMethod.p2: The template is type-checked: $event has the type of the event, a MouseEvent for click or a KeyboardEvent for keydown, and each argument must fit the parameter of the method.

whatAHandlerCannot.title: What a handler cannot contain
whatAHandlerCannot.p1: Assignments, arrow functions and more than one statement are rejected. The messages of the lexer do not always say why, so here they are, next to the handler that produces them:
whatAHandlerCannot.p2: Each of these has the same fix: a method of the component that does the work, called with the values it needs.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: Templates have no event modifiers: (keydown.enter) listens to an event whose name is literally keydown.enter, which the browser never dispatches, and the first counter never moves. Filter the key in the method, as the second field does. The same goes for preventDefault() and stopPropagation(): call them on $event.

callout2.heading: The target of $event
callout2.body: $event.target is typed EventTarget | null: the event may come from a descendant of the element, so $event.target.value does not compile. Read the field through an element ref, as in save(field.value), or narrow the target in the method.

summary.td1: Calls a method of the component, of one of its members or of an element ref, for each event.
summary.td2: Passes the event, typed by its name, or one of its properties.
summary.td3: Literals, members, variables of a loop, their properties, expressions and calls.
summary.td4: A listener active only while the condition holds. See Conditional bindings.

expressions.title: Expression syntax
expressions.lead: Interpolations, bindings, conditions and loops all take an expression: one TypeScript expression, which reads by name the public members of the component and what the template imports. Expressions can compute and combine values, but not change anything or declare functions: logic with steps belongs in the class.

whatAnExpressionCan.title: What an expression can do
whatAnExpressionCan.p1: Operators, the ternary, optional chaining and nullish coalescing, calls to methods of the component and of the values, indexes, typeof, array and object literals, spread, and the globals of the browser such as Math and JSON. An object literal needs parentheses around it: without them the interpolation renders nothing.

whatItCannotDo.title: What it cannot do
whatItCannotDo.p1: Assignments, new, functions, this, type assertions, regular expressions and more than one expression are rejected when the template is compiled:
whatItCannotDo.p2: Each of these has a place in the class: a method that assigns, a computed signal that maps a list, a member holding the result of new or of a regular expression.

whatItCanRead.title: What it can read
whatItCanRead.p1: Expressions are type-checked as code outside the class, so they see its public members and inherited ones, without this, plus the globals. The functions, constants, enums and signals of other modules are read once the template imports them (see Imports). Members marked private or protected are out of reach: expose what the template needs as public members. The checks use the options of your tsconfig.json, strict ones included.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: A member named like a global, such as history, location or name, hides the global in the template: { location } reads the member. To read the global, write window.location or globalThis.location. Inherited members hide globals the same way.

callout1.heading: Strict checks from tsconfig.json
callout1.p1: The template is checked with the strict options of the project. With noUncheckedIndexedAccess, a property of a Record may be undefined; a readonly member has the literal type of its value, so comparing it with another literal is flagged. The messages show the member with a root. prefix.

callout2.heading: Reactivity depends on where the expression is
callout2.body: Every signal an expression reads is tracked in text, conditions and loops. In an attribute, only the signal members and the imported signals the expression names are: see Binding. Event handlers follow their own, more limited syntax: see Event listeners.

for.title: Lists with @for
for.lead: @for renders its block once for each item of an array, or a number of times. Each row is identified by a key, given by track: when the array changes, the rows whose key is still there are kept, moved if needed, and only the others are created or removed.

itemsKeysAndContext.title: Items, keys and context
itemsKeysAndContext.p1: Inside the block, the item and $index, $first, $last, $even and $odd are signals: call them, as in task().title. The item updates when its row is reused for a new object with the same key, the others when rows are added or removed before, as the stripes show, without rendering the row again. Passed to a method, task() gives the item and task the signal. position = $index gives one of the variables of the position another name, which is the way to reach the index of an outer loop from an inner one.
itemsKeysAndContext.p2: The key is an expression of the item, which track reads as the block does: a property, as in track task().id, or the item itself with track task(). Without track the item itself is the key.

repeatingANumberOf.title: Repeating a number of times
repeatingANumberOf.p1: A number instead of an array repeats the block: @for (5) without a variable, or @for (step of count()) with step() going from 0 to count() - 1. The number can come from a signal, and the rows follow it.

nestedLoops.title: Nested loops
nestedLoops.p1: The inner loop sees the variables of the outer one. Both have their own $index, and the inner one hides the outer: the alias rowIndex = $index keeps the index of the row reachable from the cells.

emptyLists.title: Empty lists
emptyLists.p1: There is no @empty block: wrap the loop in an @if on the length of the array.
emptyLists.example1: A list of messages that can be empty

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: Type notes next to Ada in both columns, then move the last person to the top. Tracked by identifier, the row of Ada moves with its field and its notes. Tracked by index, each row stays where it is and shows the person now at its position: the names move, but the notes stay in place, next to someone else. Track by a stable identifier, never by index, when the rows hold state.
edgeCases.example2: An item replaced by a copy
edgeCases.p2: Replacing an item with a new object with the same key updates its row in place: the first column shows APPLE, in the same element. Tracking the item itself creates a new row for the new object, losing the state of the old one. A signal inside the item, as in the third column, updates the text without replacing the item at all.
edgeCases.example3: Two items with the same key
edgeCases.p3: A key repeated in the list gets a row per occurrence, matched in order, so the rows follow the array at every change: press the button a few times. Rows with the same key are told apart only by their order, so unique keys remain the safe choice when rows hold state.

callout1.heading: What can be iterated, and what cannot
callout1.p1: Arrays and numbers only: a Set, a Map or a string must be converted to an array first, for example with [...set] in a computed signal. There is no $count: use the length of the array. The expression of track reads the item, the implicit variables, the members of the component and the imports, but no element ref. A negative number renders nothing.

if.title: Conditionals with @if, @else if and @else
if.lead: @if renders a block only while its condition is truthy, with optional @else if and @else branches. The condition is reactive: it runs again whenever a signal it reads changes, and the block switches branch when the result says so.

branches.title: Branches
branches.p1: The conditions are tried from the top, and the first truthy one wins. Like text interpolations, conditions are always reactive, even when they call a method. A block can contain anything a template can: elements, text, components and other control flow.

whenABranchIs.title: When a branch is rendered again
whenABranchIs.p1: The block keeps track of the branch it shows, not of the value of the condition. While the same branch wins, its elements are left alone; when another branch wins, the elements of the old one are removed, with the components inside them, and the new ones are created.
whenABranchIs.p2: Type some notes, then add guests: the condition runs again at every click, but it stays true, and the field keeps its text. Go down to zero and back: the field is created again, empty. State that must survive belongs in signals, not in the elements of a branch.

callout2.heading: Syntax errors
callout2.p1: The space after @if is required, an @else must follow a block, and there is no as to name the value of the condition: read it again inside the block, or keep it in a computed signal.

callout3.heading: Truthy, not true
callout3.body: The condition follows JavaScript: 0, '', null, undefined and NaN select the @else branch. For a count that can be zero, compare it explicitly, as guests() > 0 does.

imports.title: Imports
imports.lead: @import brings into a template what it uses from other modules. The components and directives are read by the compiler at build time, which checks every use of their selectors, inputs and events against them. Any other export (a function, a constant, an enum, a class, a signal, a type) is read by the expressions and the type arguments of the template.

forms.title: Forms
forms.p1: The syntax is the one of the named imports of TypeScript: one or more names in braces, as to import one under another name, default as name for the default export, * as name for the whole module, and a path in single or double quotes. A file can export several components, and one @import brings all those the template needs. The imports come first in the template, before any other content.
forms.p2: A relative path is resolved against the template, as a file, with or without the .ts extension, or as a folder with an index.ts. Any other path is resolved as the TypeScript files of the project resolve it: the name of a package (@scope/pkg), through the exports of its package.json, or an alias of the paths of tsconfig.json (@app/models).
forms.p3: The code generated for the template imports the module of a package by the name written in the @import, as the rest of the application does: the bundler resolves it with the same conditions, and every component shares one instance of the module.

values.title: Functions, constants, enums and types
values.example1: A function, an enum and a signal from two modules
values.p1: The expressions of the template read the other exports under the name they are imported as, like the members of the component: a function is called, as { formatPrice(price, Currency.Euro) } does, a constant or an enum is read, a class is checked with instanceof, a namespace (* as utils) reads every export of its module. An event can call an imported function: (click)="addItem()".
values.p2: A module signal stays reactive: a binding reading it, or calling an exported function that reads one, is updated when it changes, like a binding reading a signal member. The browser imports only the names the expressions read: a type or an interface is only for the type-check, e.g. as a type argument, <my-list(Row)>.
values.p3: The variables of the template (the item of a @for and its aliases) hide an import named like them. A name cannot be imported if it is also a member of the component, inherited ones included: an expression reading it would be ambiguous, so import it under another name with as. root, $event and the names starting with __ are reserved by the compiler.

whenToImport.title: When to import
whenToImport.p1: Being able to import any export does not make the template the place for everything. The state of a component, and the logic that reads and changes it, live in its class whenever they belong to it: its members show what the template depends on, the class can be read and tested on its own, and the template stays a description of the view. Import in a template what really belongs to another module.
whenToImport.p2: Types are the clearest case: a type argument of a generic component or directive, <ex-list(Row)>, costs nothing at runtime. Enums and classes are worth their import in particular conditions, such as @if (task().status === Status.Archived) or @if (shape() instanceof Circle), where a member wrapping them would add nothing. Functions, constants and signals can be imported too, e.g. a formatter shared by many templates or the signals of a store, but they are not the default choice: a computed signal or a method of the class usually tells better what the component shows.
whenToImport.p3: The examples of this page and of Sharing state import functions and signals to show what the compiler supports, not because every component should be written that way.

importingIsNotRegistering.title: Importing loads the module
importingIsNotRegistering.p1: The browser knows a component only once the file declaring its class has run, which defines the custom element. The template module imports the modules of its @import statements, so each template loads what it uses and nothing else; @import lazy { Name } from '...' keeps the type-check without loading the module. See Selectors and registration, which also shows the error for a component used without @import.

callout1.heading: Errors
callout1.p1: With a path that does not resolve, a default import written without braces (write default as name) or a name the module does not export, the template does not compile. The editor reports the imports nobody uses as unnecessary, and removes them with Organize Imports.

callout2.heading: Components of compiled libraries
callout2.body: A package compiled to JavaScript publishes declaration files (.d.ts), which keep no decorator: its functions, constants, enums, classes and types can be imported in a template, its components and directives not yet. The components of a package that publishes its TypeScript sources, of a package of the same monorepo, or reached through an alias, are imported like the local ones.

callout3.heading: Const enums
callout3.body: A const enum exists only for TypeScript: its module does not export it at runtime, so a template can name it in a type argument but not read it in an expression. Use a regular enum, or an object declared as const.

callout4.heading: Reactivity of compiled packages
callout4.body: A signal exported by a compiled package is recognized from its type in the declarations (Signal<number>), and stays reactive. The body of its functions is not part of the declarations: an attribute binding calling one is evaluated once, even if the function reads a signal. Wrap the call in a computed member of the class.

overview.title: Template syntax
overview.lead: A Xaendar template is HTML with a handful of additions: interpolations and bindings in braces, events in parentheses, control flow and imports introduced by @, and directives. The compiler reads it at build time, checks every expression against the class of the component, and turns it into code that creates the DOM and wires each node to the signals it reads.

everythingAtAGlance.td1: A text node showing the value
everythingAtAGlance.td3: An attribute, or the input of a component
everythingAtAGlance.td10: Bindings applied only while a condition holds

stricterThanHtml.title: Stricter than HTML
stricterThanHtml.p1: The browser forgives a lot of HTML; the compiler does not, and each of these mistakes fails the build with the position of the problem:
stricterThanHtml.li1: void elements are closed with /> as in XML, <input />, never left open;
stricterThanHtml.li2: closing tags match the opening ones letter by letter, upper case included;
stricterThanHtml.li3: attribute values are always in double quotes.

whitespace.title: Whitespace
whitespace.p1: Line breaks and indentation inside a text are kept, as in HTML, and the browser collapses them into one space. The compiler drops the text made only of whitespace when it holds a line break, as between tags on separate lines, while a space between two tags or two interpolations on the same line stays.
whitespace.example1: Five ways of writing two words
whitespace.li1: the line break between two words becomes a space;
whitespace.li2: the line break between two tags is dropped, with the indentation around it;
whitespace.li4: the space between two interpolations on the same line stays;
whitespace.li5: building the text in one expression keeps it.

specialCharacters.title: Special characters
specialCharacters.p1: @, braces and < have a meaning in templates. To show them, write a character reference, as in HTML, or interpolate a string. Character references are decoded in texts and attribute values, so © shows ©; for the other characters, such as arrows and typographic quotes, you can also write the character itself.

callout1.heading: An @ in plain text
callout1.p1: An @ followed by letters starts a block, so an email address in the text does not compile: write @ instead. Inside attribute values @ is safe.

callout2.heading: A less-than sign in plain text
callout2.p1: < always opens a tag, and the error points somewhere after it: write < instead. > is safe.

callout3.heading: An unclosed comment
callout3.p1: HTML comments are allowed and are not rendered. One that is never closed stops the compilation with Comment never closed.

callout4.heading: Upper-case tags
callout4.body: <DIV> with </DIV> compiles and renders a div, as in HTML; only the two tags have to match.

svgMathml.title: SVG and MathML
svgMathml.lead: SVG and MathML can be written straight into templates. The compiler knows which elements belong to them and creates each one in the right namespace, so everything a template does with HTML works with them too: bindings, events, control flow, components around them.

svg.title: SVG
svg.p1: The bars are real SVGRectElements: an @for renders them, their geometry comes from a computed signal, and their listeners are typed as for HTML, with a MouseEvent for mouseenter. Names written in camelCase, such as viewBox or linearGradient, are kept as they are, as SVG requires. Styles apply as usual: the stylesheet of the component colors the bars and the hovered one.
svg.p2: In SVG, <foreignObject> holds HTML: the compiler creates its children in the HTML namespace, so the paragraph is an HTMLParagraphElement rendered as HTML, while the <foreignObject> itself and the elements after it stay in SVG.

mathml.title: MathML
mathml.p1: The elements inside <math> are MathMLElements, rendered by the browser. Interpolations inside <mn> and <mi> update like any text: move the slider and only the numbers change.

callout1.heading: Attributes are strings
callout1.body: As for HTML, a binding sets an attribute with setAttribute: numbers become strings, which SVG accepts for geometry. Properties of SVG elements, such as animated values, have to be set in code.

switch.title: Branching with @switch
switch.lead: @switch compares one value with a list of cases and renders the block of the first one that matches, or the @default block when none does. It reads better than a chain of @else if when every branch tests the same value.

cases.title: Cases
cases.p1: The comparison is strict, ===: @case (1) does not match the string '1'. Cases written one after the other without a block share the block of the last one, as pending and paid do. As with @if, the block is rendered again only when another case wins.

edgeCases.title: Edge cases
edgeCases.p1: As in JavaScript, @default is rendered only when no case matches, wherever it is written: in the second column it comes first, and the matching case still wins. Writing it last keeps the template easier to read.
edgeCases.example2: How many times the value is read
edgeCases.p2: The expression of the switch runs once each time the switch is evaluated, whatever case matches: once for Monday, and once for the weekend too. A method with side effects, or a slow one, is not repeated for every case it is compared with.

callout1.heading: Case values are literals
callout1.p1: The value of a case cannot read the members of the component. Compare with literals, or move the logic into a computed signal that returns one of them.
